The failure notices go to one GitHub issue per unit; a repeat failure adds a comment rather than a new issue. Nothing closes the issue when the unit recovers, so close it by hand. The notices run on onclappc02 itself, so if that host is down no issue is filed; only the daily GitHub Actions checks still run. Every scheduled job and its badge is listed in CI & scheduled jobs.
Credentials for the sync and purge scripts come from Secret Manager into a gitignored .env in the bioc-edge checkout (./make-env.sh). Splitting the production units away from dev checkouts, and automating detection and routine fixes, is planned in bioc-infrastructure#43.

title: Operations: who runs what, runbooks, open decisions
text:
Runbooks
All commands run from the bioc-edge checkout on onclappc02 unless stated. For commands that call the Cloudflare API, load the credentials first:
./make-env.sh && set -a && . ./.env && set +a
None of these procedures has been rehearsed on production as a drill. The M1 item “Rollback rehearsed and written up” is still open on the roadmap.

Deploy the Worker
Deploys are manual; there is no deploy from CI yet (an open M0 item).

Note the version that is live now, so you can return to it: cd worker && npx wrangler deployments list
Deploy: just deploy-worker (runs npx wrangler deploy in worker/). The routes come from worker/wrangler.jsonc, and a deploy replaces the Worker’s routes with that list, so a route added in the dashboard disappears on the next deploy.
Check: curl -sI https://bioconductor.org/ | grep -iE '^server|cf-cache-status|x-bioc-build' shows server: cloudflare, and a package index still answers: curl -sI https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/src/contrib/PACKAGES.
Run the probe now rather than waiting for tomorrow’s: gh workflow run health.yml -R seandavi/bioc-edge.



Roll back the Worker

cd worker && npx wrangler deployments list and pick the last good version ID.
npx wrangler rollback <version-id> -m "<reason>".
Check as in step 3 above. A rollback changes which Worker version runs; R2 content, _routes.json and the edge cache are untouched.



Roll back the site build
The Worker serves whichever build _routes.json names. "latest" follows the site/latest pointer that bioc-website CI moves on every main build.

Find the last good build sha: gh run list -R seandavi/bioc-website -w site.yml -b main (each successful run published site/<headSha>/).
Write the route table with that sha pinned:
echo '{"build": "<good sha>", "prefixes": ["/"]}' > routes.json
npx wrangler r2 object put bioc-site/_routes.json --file routes.json --remote
Within about a minute, curl -sI https://bioconductor.org/ | grep x-bioc-build shows the pinned sha. No purge is needed: build pages are cached under their build’s sha.
To undo, write {"build": "latest", "prefixes": ["/"]} the same way. While the pin is in place, new main builds publish but are not served.

An empty prefixes list, or no _routes.json, makes the mirror serve everything: the legacy pages copied from master. That is the fallback if no build is good.


A failed sync
A failed bioc-sync opens (or comments on) the issue bioc-sync.service is failing in bioc-edge, with the run’s journal and log files.

Read the issue, or journalctl --user -u bioc-sync.service -n 100.
If rsync failed (the log says “aborting before touching R2”), nothing in R2 changed. Fix the cause (the log and .err file say what rsync hit), then run one now: systemctl --user start bioc-sync.service. Rsync exits 23 and 24 (unreadable or vanished files) are expected and do not fail the run.
If the run failed after uploading started, the next run does not retry files it already pulled. Run the checksum pass, which reports what is missing or different in R2 and prints the rclone copy command that re-uploads it: systemctl --user start bioc-reconcile.service. It hashes the whole local mirror and takes hours (the unit allows 12); it holds the mirror lock, so hourly syncs skip while it runs.
If the purge step failed, the files are in R2 but the edge may still serve old copies. Purge the keys from the run’s log (below).
When a run succeeds (systemctl --user status bioc-sync.service), close the issue.

A missed hour is caught up by the timer (Persistent=true). bioc-reconcile failing to get the lock within two hours also files an issue.


Purge the edge cache
The hourly sync purges what it changes, so a manual purge is for when that did not happen.
. ./cf-purge.sh
cf_purge_keys packages/3.23/bioc/src/contrib/PACKAGES   # storage keys: 3.23, not release
cf_purge_keys purges each key on all four hosts in both zones. Check with curl -sI for cf-cache-status: MISS. The rate limit is shared with the running sync; read Purging on the edge-cache page before purging more than a few hundred URLs or a whole zone.


Pull a bad package
The mirror in R2 follows master: the hourly sync copies master with deletions, so a file removed from master is deleted from R2 and purged on the next run, together with the updated PACKAGES. The lasting fix is removing the package on master, which is the core team’s BBS process, not something this stack controls.
If users must stop receiving the file before that happens:

Delete each copy from R2 by its storage key (numeric version, not release; source tarball and each binary are separate keys): rclone delete r2:bioc-site/packages/3.23/bioc/src/contrib/<pkg>_<ver>.tar.gz
Purge the same keys: cf_purge_keys packages/3.23/bioc/src/contrib/<pkg>_<ver>.tar.gz.
Check the URL returns 404.

What this does and does not do, from how sync.sh works (checked 2026-09-30; not yet done on production):

PACKAGES still lists the package until master’s index changes, so installs fail with a download error instead of installing the bad file.
The hourly sync uploads only files that changed on master, so it does not put the file back unless master’s copy changes. The weekly reconcile will list it as missing from R2; do not run the re-upload command it prints for that key.
Mirrors that already synced the file keep it.



Roll back DNS
The Route53 zone and CloudFront are kept as the rollback target, and records are frozen until 2026-10-12: change no DNS record in either zone, or make the same change in both.

The Worker is the problem, DNS is fine: switch the bioconductor.org and www records to DNS only in the Cloudflare dashboard. Traffic goes straight to CloudFront and  the legacy servers within 300 s. Steps: flip the site, rollback.
Cloudflare’s DNS service is the problem: put the Route53 nameservers back at the registrar. Most resolvers follow within an hour, some take a day. Steps and the four nameservers: change the nameservers.

Both depend on master and CloudFront still running, which they will until M2.

Top risks

One operator, no backup. Every component in the table above with a named operator, except the legacy servers, has the same one. Access, credentials and the knowledge of these runbooks sit with one person.
A personal Cloudflare account holds the zone, the Worker and the R2 bucket. The account migration is deferred, and nobody is named to own the new account.

title: Propagation in the legacy system: the nebbiolo1 rule and the push hooks
text:
NotePart of the migration record



A dated snapshot kept as history, not a live view of the current system: corrected if wrong, but not updated to track the estate. The rule that decides what the new system publishes is on the propagation gate; this page describes the gate that still feeds bioconductor.org, and the constraints any replacement inherits from it.

title: Propagation in the legacy system: the nebbiolo1 rule and the push hooks
text:
The rule
Paraphrased:

r-universe does not care about R CMD check; we do — that is the first big difference. And they build and propagate on any new commit, regardless of a version bump. So right now we match on the sha and version of the nebbiolo1 build to r-universe, because that Linux host still has all our pre-hooks valid — preventing bad version numbers, large files, and the rest that we also check. And then we make sure the check is actually clean.

So the gate is three conditions, not one:

the r-universe build’s version matches what nebbiolo1 built,
its source commit sha matches too, and
the check is clean.

title: Propagation in the legacy system: the nebbiolo1 rule and the push hooks
text:
Why it keys on nebbiolo1
The sha match looks redundant next to the version match, and the choice of nebbiolo1 specifically looks arbitrary. Neither is.
Bioconductor’s push-time checks are gitolite server-side hooks on git.bioconductor.org (see The pre-hooks below). r-universe does not build from gitolite — it builds from a GitHub mirror, because it requires a GitHub remote. nebbiolo1 builds from canonical git.
Matching the sha against nebbiolo1 is therefore a provenance check wearing the costume of an equality check. It establishes that the commit came through the git server, and so had the pre-hooks applied to it. Bioconductor inherits that guarantee without re-running anything.





flowchart LR
  DEV["maintainer push"] --> HOOKS{"gitolite pre-hooks<br/>version rules · 5 MiB limit<br/>merge markers"}
  HOOKS -->|rejected| X["push fails"]
  HOOKS -->|accepted| GIT["git.bioconductor.org<br/>canonical source"]
  GIT --> MIRROR["GitHub mirror<br/>github.com/bioc/*"]
  GIT --> NEB["nebbiolo1<br/>R CMD build / check"]
  MIRROR --> RU["r-universe<br/>build + R CMD check + BiocCheck"]
  NEB --> GATE{"gate<br/>sha + version match<br/>check clean"}
  RU --> GATE
  GATE -->|pass| WEB["bioconductor.org"]
  GATE -->|hold| NOP["not propagated"]

  classDef g fill:#f3fbf4,stroke:#3d8b47,color:#12263f
  classDef r fill:#fdf0ef,stroke:#b4453c,color:#12263f
  classDef n fill:#eef4ff,stroke:#4a6fa5,color:#12263f
  class GIT,NEB,WEB g
  class X,NOP r
  class MIRROR,RU n






The practical consequence: a gate that runs outside this path must replace the provenance guarantee, either by verifying the sha traces back to canonical git or by re-implementing the hooks. The former is cheaper and more faithful.

title: Propagation in the legacy system: the nebbiolo1 rule and the push hooks

How closely does r-universe agree with nebbiolo1?
This is the load-bearing question for any plan that lets r-universe’s check stand in for BBS’s, so it was measured rather than assumed.
Comparing r-universe’s linux-release-x86_64 job against nebbiolo1’s checksrc stage in BUILD_STATUS_DB.txt for release 3.23, across all 2,416 packages present in both, excluding the 90 where BBS skipped the check or r-universe had no job:

title: Propagation in the legacy system: the nebbiolo1 rule and the push hooks
text:
The pre-hooks
Public, at Bioconductor/git-hooks. Two caveats before trusting any of it:

The default devel branch is stale Python 2. The live code is almost certainly the ConvertToPython3 branch, which was never merged. Which branch is actually deployed could not be confirmed — that needs access to the git server itself.
A server-side hooks.conf can disable any hook per package. Its contents are not public. These are defaults, not guarantees.

File size (prevent_large_files.py): exactly 5,242,880 bytes (5 MiB, strict >), raised from 5,000,000 decimal in August 2020. Applies to software packages only — data experiment, workflow and book packages are not size-gated by the hook. The implementation sizes files at the push tip rather than walking the push range, so a large blob added and deleted within one push passes.
Version numbers (prevent_bad_version_numbers.py): format must match ^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$, then:







Branch
Rule




RELEASE_*
x unchanged; y unchanged and even; z non-decreasing


devel
x unchanged; y odd; y unchanged unless 99; z non-decreasing unless y is 99



Two properties matter for the gate. The hook never requires a bump — a push with no version change is accepted, and that acceptance is exactly what makes “no bump, no propagation” the gate’s job rather than the hook’s. And the hook has no knowledge of the current Bioconductor release number; it enforces parity and stability, not “y matches this cycle.”
The parity rule holds almost perfectly in practice. Across the release universe, 2,398 of 2,399 packages have an even y. The single exception is BiocVersion 3.23.1, whose version is the Bioconductor version — so any reimplementation needs one hardcoded exception.
Also present: a merge-conflict-marker check (known leaky — git-hooks#2) and a duplicate-commit check that is pure SVN-transition legacy and can be dropped. Force-push and branch-creation restrictions come from gitolite ACLs rather than hooks; GitHub branch protection covers those natively.

BiocCheck does not substitute for the hooks
Since r-universe runs BiocCheck, it is tempting to treat that as covering the pre-hooks. It does not:



Hook rule
BiocCheck
Covered?




5,242,880-byte file limit
.MAX_FILE_SIZE <- 5e+6L, emits WARNING
No — different threshold, different severity, and it does not fire at all on tarball input, which is how r-universe runs it


version parity
checkVersionNumber(), emits WARNING
Partial and weaker


x unchanged, y unchanged, z non-decreasing
—
No. Structurally impossible: BiocCheck never sees the previous version


merge markers
—
No



That last row is the useful one. A gate does have the previous version — it is already in the state it keeps for delta detection — so it is naturally positioned to enforce exactly the rules BiocCheck cannot, at no extra data cost.
If the size check is ported, Bioconductor/BiocContributions’ scripts/validate.py already uses 5 * 1024 * 1024, matching the hook exactly.

title: Propagation in the legacy system: the nebbiolo1 rule and the push hooks
section: How a replacement gate was first sketched
text:
How a replacement gate was first sketched






Note



Written 2026-08-04, before the pilot existed. Kept because it records the reasoning; the pilot gate that was actually built is a Cloudflare Worker, not this workflow, and differs in the ways that page lists.


Given the above, the job is a reconciler over metadata, not a check farm: no matrix, no re-running checks, no webhook receiver.
on:
  schedule: [{cron: '55 * * * *'}]   # after r-universe's :41 sync has had time to build
  workflow_dispatch:
jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: python3 gate.py          # diff vs state, evaluate, rewrite state
      - run: |
          git add state/gate.json
          git diff --cached --quiet || { git commit -m "gate $(date -u +%FT%TZ)"; git push; }
Per changed package, gate.py evaluates: version-diff rules against its own state, check outcome from _jobs, BiocCheck counts from _bioccheck, _failure for the stale-green case, and sha provenance. State lives in a committed file rather than the Actions cache — it survives past the cache’s seven-day eviction, and git log becomes a free audit trail answering “why did this propagate.”

Two modes, and the order to build them in
Shadow. BBS stays authoritative; the workflow only reconciles r-universe against BUILD_STATUS_DB.txt and reports disagreements. Every input is public, so this needs no builder access and no Bioconductor-side change. It also supplies the check-status axis that model-binary-flow.py currently lacks.
Reference. Actions runs the canonical Linux check itself and becomes what nebbiolo1 is now. This is the mode that actually retires a builder — and where the 59-vs-18 divergence has to be explained rather than merely measured.
Shadow first, and let the divergence data decide whether reference mode is safe.

title: Propagation in the legacy system: the nebbiolo1 rule and the push hooks
text:
What could not be determined

Whether checksrc: WARNINGS counts as “clean” for propagation. 391 packages — 16% of the repo — sit in that state. The answer changes whether the gate reads as ~77% or ~93% permissive. This is a question for the Bioconductor core team, not something to infer.
Which branch of git-hooks is deployed, and the contents of the per-package hooks.conf that can disable individual hooks.
Measured commit-to-build latency. It is bounded below by the hourly sync cron, but no primary source gives a wall-clock figure.

title: Bioconductor Infrastructure
text:
TL;DR
Since 2026-09-28, bioconductor.org is served by the new stack. The replacement estate is a set of repos that meet at data contracts rather than shared machines, which is why each can proceed — or be replaced — without stopping the others.



Repo
What it is
Retires
Status




bioc-registry
The data plane: an r-universe observer plus the propagation gate that decides which build is fit to publish and what is true about a package, exposed as an installable repository and a Parquet archive. It publishes at its own host; bioconductor.org does not serve from it yet (registry switch)
Planned: the three builders and the legacy build system. Today bioconductor.org’s packages still come from BBS and r-universe through master (how it works)



bioc-website
The builder: a Python pipeline and an Astro static build that render package truth into ~93,000 pages, published immutably by CI

How the pieces meet

  master -- "bioc-sync, hourly" --> mir[("R2: the mirror")]
  site["bioc-website<br/>static build, CI"] --> b[("R2: site/<sha>")]
  mir --> wk["bioc-edge Worker<br/>build first, else mirror"]
  b --> wk
  wk --> v(["bioconductor.org"])

Solid lines to bioconductor.org are the path that serves it today: packages come from master through the hourly sync, and the registry is not in that path. Dashed lines are the registry’s own outputs and the planned switch. Detail: how bioconductor.org works.
The organising principle is one idea applied at two scales: define where the data comes from once, and let every consumer render it. Inside bioc-website that shows up as the astro/data/ seam between its pipeline and its renderer. Across the estate it shows up as the table above. The website is one consumer of package truth. It is deliberately not the place where “what is true about a package” gets decided.

title: Bioconductor Infrastructure
text:
The contracts
Everything above holds together at five seams. They are worth stating in one place, because each is a place where a change in one repo can quietly break another.
1. astro/data/ — pipeline to renderer, inside bioc-website. JSON written to disk by a Python pipeline, read by an Astro build. Nothing downstream knows where the data came from; nothing upstream knows how it is rendered. That seam is what let the same component render both the legacy-parity pages and the new data-plane-fed pages unchanged.
2. The registry’s HTTP API — data plane to website, fetched at build time from /data/prop/{universe}/index.json, /data/state/{universe}/latest, and /prop/{universe}/cas/{sha256}. This is what the /next/ pages render: what propagated, not whatever r-universe last built.
3. The R2 object layout — build to serving. The website’s CI writes immutable site/<sha>/ builds, a site/latest pointer, and preview/pr-<n>/ for every pull request (served at /_pr/<n>/). The Worker reads them. The build side publishes; the serving side decides what is served — write access to the website repo never implies the power to change production.
4. The route table — _routes.json, an object in R2, not code. Flipping a route from mirrored legacy content to a static build is a data write; rolling it back is the same write in reverse. No deploy, no rebuild. An empty table means the mirror serves everything, which is the safe default. Since the cutover the table routes / to the latest build: the build serves any path it has a file for, and the mirror copy in R2 serves the rest.
5. Request logs — serving to statistics. The Worker emits one structured record per request in the same field vocabulary as the CloudFront logs it replaces, delivered by Logpush to Google Cloud Storage, so both eras can be one query rather than a migration project. Analysis lives in bioc-traffic. The record keeps the raw client address; de-identification is a view, and nothing published carries the address (ADR 0012).

title: Bioconductor Infrastructure
text:
Where this stands
The serving replacement took over bioconductor.org on 2026-09-28: nameservers moved to Cloudflare in the afternoon and the site followed that evening (DNS runbook). The legacy servers still run behind it, and still produce the content it mirrors, until milestone M2 retires them. Package landing pages exist for 35 releases: 3.23 and 3.24 are regenerated, and the 33 older releases are a frozen snapshot (ADR 0006, site build). The build-system track is earlier. Software source tarballs are still built by BBS and most binaries by r-universe; serving them from the registry instead is the registry switch. Annotation, experiment-data and workflow packages have no replacement builder running yet (bioc-build is a proof of concept).
Numbers throughout this site are point-in-time measurements, not live dashboards — check the date on each page before relying on specifics.

Two costs, not one
Two figures appear across these pages and they are not competing estimates of the same thing:

~$5,000/month is the AWS estate being retired — CloudFront, the S3 bucket, and the master and staging webservers — before counting the builder hardware or the staff time to keep three operating systems patched.
$240-500/month is the estimate for the Cloudflare stack replacing it, from production traffic on 2026-09-28. Storage is about $77 of that (5.1 TB in R2); the rest is per-request charges. R2 charges no egress fees, and egress is most of the difference (details).



Known weak points
Stated here rather than discovered later:

The website reads the registry’s stored JSON shape directly, not a versioned API. An unreachable endpoint fails the build loudly, which is right; a renamed field renders a blank section on a page and fails nothing. The convention is “never change a shape in place, add fields and tolerate absences” — it is a convention, with no mechanism behind it.
astro/data/ has no written schema. Its shape is implied by the code that writes it and the code that reads it, and by nothing else.
The 15-minute poll has no fast alerting. A silent stop is caught by bioc-registry’s daily freshness check, which fails when the latest observation is more than 36 hours old (the freshness badge above).
One person operates the new stack, with no named backup, on a personal Cloudflare account and one host. This and the other operational risks are on operations.
Some facts are written in several places — release numbers, repository lists, display labels — and at least one set of display labels already disagrees with itself.

text:
How this site is organised
The sidebar groups pages by reader and by how they are kept:

They are corrected if they were wrong at the time, not updated to track the system; a status banner points to the current page. What the new site has changed is the one record that is appended to.
Decisions (ADRs) record the reasoning, including decisions later reversed. They are not edited; a new ADR supersedes an old one.







Note



This site is deliberately public, so that the people affected by this work can read it without needing an account or an invitation. Findings are shared with the Bioconductor core team as they land, so read these pages as work in progress rather than settled conclusions.

text:
Reference page, checked 2026-09-30. It describes the running system; if something here is wrong, that is a bug in this page. Sources: the Worker in bioc-edge (worker/src/index.ts, keys.ts, sync.sh), bioc-website’s site.yml, and live responses from bioconductor.org.
Since 2026-09-28 (about 20:09 UTC) bioconductor.org is answered by a Cloudflare Worker, bioc-site, reading from an R2 bucket, also named bioc-site. The legacy server master.bioconductor.org still runs and still produces the package repositories; the edge copies them every hour. The registry does not serve bioconductor.org yet.

title: How bioconductor.org Works
text:
Terms
Other pages use these words with these meanings.



Term
Meaning




master
master.bioconductor.org, the legacy web server. Its docroot is where BBS and the core team’s propagation put the package repositories. The mirror is copied from it. It stays up until parity is clean (roadmap M2).


the mirror
The copy of master’s docroot in R2, at the top level of the bioc-site bucket (packages/..., checkResults/...). About 5.1 TB.


the build
One output of bioc-website’s Astro build, stored at site/<sha>-<snapshot hash>/ in R2. site/latest holds the id of the newest main or dispatched build.


preview
A pull request’s build, stored at preview/pr-<n>/ and served at /_pr/<n>/. The R2 key and the URL differ.


the edge
The bioc-site Worker plus Cloudflare’s cache in front of R2. The code is in bioc-edge.


route table
_routes.json in R2: which URL prefixes the build answers before the mirror. Data, not code.


symlink map
_symlinks.json in R2: master’s symlinks (packages/release → 3.23, the R-version aliases under contrib/), which object storage cannot hold.


the sync
bioc-sync, the hourly systemd job that copies master into the mirror.


BBS
The Bioconductor Build System on the legacy build machines. It builds the source tarballs.


r-universe
r-universe.dev’s bioc and bioc-release universes. They build most of the Windows and macOS binaries on bioconductor.org.


the registry
bioc-registry: observes r-universe, applies the propagation gate, and publishes its own repository at its own workers.dev host. Not in the serving path.


parity
The daily comparison of bioconductor.org with master, path by path (bioc-edge parity.yml).


the manifest
The mirror’s file list at /api/v1/manifest/, used by mirror operators.

title: How bioconductor.org Works
section: Serving: how a request is answered
text:
Serving: how a request is answered

Hosts
All four hostnames go to the same Worker and read the same bucket, so they serve the same content (checked 2026-09-30: all four return build 360bb871 at /).



Host
Zone
Use




bioconductor.org
bioconductor.org (Cloudflare nameservers since 2026-09-28 17:30 UTC)
Production


www.bioconductor.org
bioconductor.org
Production


next.bioconductor.org
bioconductor.org
Same content as production


bioc-dev.cancerdatasci.org
cancerdatasci.org (Worker custom domain)
PR previews at /_pr/<n>/. /_pr/ also answers on production hosts today (bioc-edge#48).



The Route53 zone is kept as the rollback target, with a record freeze until 2026-10-12 (DNS runbook).


The route table: build first, then the mirror
The route table in production is:
{"build": "latest", "prefixes": ["/"]}
Every path is routed, so for each request the Worker tries the build’s files (site/<latest sha>/...) first and the mirror’s files second. The build wins wherever it has a file; anything it lacks (package tarballs, PACKAGES, checkResults, old-release pages) comes from the mirror. A response served from the build carries an x-bioc-build: <sha> header; a mirror response has none. The Worker rereads _routes.json and site/latest at most once a minute per isolate, so a new build or a rollback reaches all traffic within about a minute. Pinning build to an older sha is the rollback.


Request order
The Worker handles a request in this order (bioc-edge worker/src/index.ts, Worker version 3d1ad785, deployed 2026-09-29):

Anything other than GET or HEAD gets 405.
/packages/stats/...: the .tab files, the HTML pages and static/barchart.js are read from R2, where bioc-traffic uploads them daily. A key missing from R2 is a 404 (download stats).
/_pr/<n>/... serves that PR’s preview, and /_latest/... serves the latest build. Paths the preview lacks fall back to production. Neither is cached, and links in the HTML are rewritten to stay under the prefix.
The redirect table (redirects.json, generated from master’s .htaccess of 2026-07-30) answers with one 301.
Book short URLs (/books/<name>) get a 302 to the release or devel book.
Edge cache lookup (see Caching).
R2: build keys, then mirror keys, with symlinks resolved through the symlink map.
On a miss: a generated directory listing for a few prefixes, or a 302 for a package short URL (/packages/<name>), or a 404 whose body is the site’s 404 page (help/404/index.html, since 2026-09-29).

/solr/ is not served (it returns 404). Before the Worker runs, a Cloudflare WAF rule blocks AS150436 and AS4229 on /talks/, the crawler found on 2026-09-28 (what the new site has changed).


Caching
Detail, keys and the purge procedure are on Edge cache. In short:

Cached at the edge: package files and repository metadata (PACKAGES, VIEWS, config.yaml, tarballs), pages from the build (keyed by build sha, so a new build invalidates them), old-release files from the archive copy (never purged), and 404s for 10 minutes (keyed by build sha).
Not cached: HTML that comes from the mirror (checkResults, old-release pages), previews, and /packages/stats/ (read from R2 on every request).
Freshness: the edge keeps objects for up to a year (s-maxage=31536000); every sync purges the objects it changed on all four hosts. Browsers get max-age=300 by default, 30 seconds for PACKAGES and config.yaml, and one year (immutable) for tarballs and zips, whose names carry the version. Browser Cache TTL is set to respect these headers in both zones.

Measured 2026-09-29 16:00-18:00 UTC: about 4,400 requests per minute, no 5xx, 63% edge hits. A miss took 200 ms from the US west coast and up to 800 ms from Europe, Asia and South America.

title: How bioconductor.org Works
text:
Publishing: how content gets there
Two independent paths write to R2. Neither goes through the registry.





flowchart LR

    RU["r-universe<br/>most binaries"] -- "core team propagation" --> M
    M -- "bioc-sync, hourly<br/>rsync + upload + purge" --> MIR[("R2: the mirror")]
  end
  subgraph SITE[Site, on merge or upstream content push]
    UP["Bioconductor/bioconductor.org<br/>prose, assets"] -- "bioc-site-refresh, 20 min<br/>snapshot + dispatch" --> GH
    GH["bioc-website main"] -- "CI: tests, Astro build" --> B[("R2: site/<sha>-<data><br/>+ site/latest")]
  end
  MIR --> W["bioc-site Worker<br/>build first, else mirror"]

  W --> V(["bioconductor.org"])
  REG["bioc-registry<br/>own workers.dev host"] -. "planned: registry switch" .-> MIR







Packages



Package type
Built by
Reaches bioconductor.org via




Software, source tarballs
BBS
master, then the sync


Software, Windows and macOS binaries
mostly r-universe, published to master by the core team’s propagation
master, then the sync


Annotation, experiment-data and workflow packages
the legacy side; no replacement is running (bioc-build is a proof of concept)
master, then the sync



The sync (bioc-sync, bioc-edge) runs hourly with up to 10 minutes of random delay, on onclappc02 from a development checkout of bioc-edge. Each run:

rsyncs master’s docroot into /data/davsean/bioc-cloudflare/mirror; 
uploads the changed files to R2 and publishes the symlink map;
regenerates the manifest;
purges the changed objects from the edge cache on all four hosts.

A weekly job, bioc-reconcile (Sunday 04:00), checks R2 against the local copy by checksum. Both open a GitHub issue on failure (CI & scheduled jobs).
So a package update reaches bioconductor.org at the next sync after it lands on master: up to about 70 minutes, plus however long that run takes. Separating these jobs from the development checkouts is planned in bioc-infrastructure#43.
The registry publishes a gated r-universe repository at its own host. No request to bioconductor.org reads from it; its data reaches the site only through the snapshot, for the experimental /next/ package pages. Making it the source of the software repositories is the registry switch, a plan with open decisions.


The site
The site content means the pages bioc-website renders plus the documents they link to: prose pages, events, site assets, and package data for the live releases. The package repositories are not part of it. Exactly what it covers, where each part is written, and how it should be managed are open for discussion in bioc-infrastructure#91 (sub-issues #92 to #95).
bioc-website’s CI (site.yml) runs on every push to main, every pull request, and on dispatch:

Pipeline tests.
Pull the data snapshot _ci/site-data.tar.zst from R2.
Astro build (the build step took 27-29 s in recent runs).
main or dispatch: upload to site/<sha>-<snapshot hash>/, then write that id to site/latest. Pull request: upload to preview/pr-<n>/, which is deleted when the PR closes.

Live pages carry the id as x-bioc-build. It includes the snapshot hash because the edge cache keys on the build id and treats builds as immutable, so new data on the same commit must get a new id. Re-running a build does not refresh cached pages (#90).
A merge to main is live within about a minute of CI finishing, because the route table follows site/latest. The snapshot has three parts, which are refreshed differently:



Part
Source
Refreshed




Prose pages, events, announcement (data/site) and site chrome (public/: style, images, js)
Bioconductor/bioconductor.org devel
Automatically. bioc-site-refresh (CI & scheduled jobs) checks every 20 minutes and, when devel has moved, regenerates this part and dispatches a build. An upstream push is live about 12 minutes later


Package data for 3.23 and 3.24 (data/<release>)
r-universe, tarball DESCRIPTIONs, download stats, biocViews
By hand only (bioc-website#5); bioc-site-refresh carries it over unchanged


Documents under upstream assets/ (PDFs such as TAB minutes)
Bioconductor/bioconductor.org
Not in the snapshot. The legacy staging cron deploys them to master, then bioc-sync copies them to R2 (#93)



Package landing pages for 3.23 and 3.24 take versions and download links from the repositories’ own PACKAGES indexes as of that snapshot (bioc-website#31); the 33 older releases are frozen.

title: How bioconductor.org Works
text:
When something looks wrong

A page looks different from before: check x-bioc-build on the response. Present means the build answered; compare with master (curl -sI https://master.bioconductor.org/<path>). Known differences are bioc-edge #43-#46.
A package update is missing: check master first. If master has it and more than 70 minutes have passed, the sync may have failed (look for its issue in bioc-edge), or the edge is holding a stale copy (Edge cache).
Report it: where to file issues.

text:
What M1 actually changes
Two records carry the entire cutover:









Hostname
Type
Current target
Note

A, Route53 Alias
d3hzwifbu1gvt4.cloudfront.net.

A, Route53 Alias
bioconductor.org.
Aliases to the apex, not to CloudFront directly



Both are live and serve the production site (“Bioconductor - Home”) today. Everything else in the zone is satellite: conference sites, mailing-list infrastructure, build machines, DKIM keys. None of it needs to change for the site itself to move — it either already points off AWS, or points at AWS/Jetstream2 resources this cutover doesn’t touch.

The apex is the hard part
Route53 “Alias” records — the mechanism used for the apex today — only resolve to AWS resources (CloudFront, ELB, S3, another record in the same zone, etc.). They cannot target an arbitrary external host like bioc-dev.cancerdatasci.org, and a plain CNAME isn’t legal at a zone apex per the DNS spec. www.bioconductor.org doesn’t have this problem — it’s not the apex, so it can become a normal CNAME to the new edge once the zone is ready. Decision (2026-09-17): move the zone’s nameservers to Cloudflare. Cloudflare flattens a CNAME at the apex, so the apex can target the Worker directly, and AWS leaves the DNS path entirely. The domain registration stays at AWS; only the nameservers change.
Rejected: a thin CloudFront distribution as a pass-through, origin set to bioc-dev.cancerdatasci.org, with the Route53 Alias repointed at it. It moves no records, but keeps AWS in the request path indefinitely and adds a cache-miss origin-fetch charge (~$0.02/GB) on top of viewer egress.

2. Change the nameservers

2a. Lower the Route53 NS TTL — at least 2 days before 2b
After a nameserver change, a resolver keeps using the old nameservers until its cached NS record expires. There are two copies of that record: the .org registry’s (3600 s, not ours to change) and the one the old provider serves itself, which some resolvers prefer. So each direction’s tail is set by the provider being left:








Direction
TTLs that matter
Worst-case tail




Switch to Cloudflare (2b)
.org 1 h; Route53 NS — 172800 s today, 3600 s after this step
2 days → 1 hour


Roll back to Route53
.org 1 h; Cloudflare NS, 86400 s
1 day, whatever we do here



This step shortens the switch, not a rollback. Cloudflare’s NS TTL is adjustable only as part of Foundation DNS (Enterprise), so on this zone it is fixed at a day. The step is still worth doing for two reasons:

It shrinks the window in which Route53 and Cloudflare must both be kept correct.
It makes a second attempt after a rollback clean. Resolvers that re-fetch Route53’s NS during a rollback cache it for the full TTL, so without this step the retry starts a fresh 2-day tail.

A TTL is a ceiling, not a wait. Each resolver’s clock started at its last fetch, many follow the parent’s 1 hour, and some cap long TTLs. So most traffic moves within about an hour either way, and the worst-case figures describe the last stragglers.
This changes no answers, only how long they are cached. It is safe to do any time.
In the AWS console (account 555219204010, the NIH DNS role):

Open Route 53 → Hosted zones (https://us-east-1.console.aws.amazon.com/route53/v2/hostedzones).
Click bioconductor.org (hosted zone ID Z2LMJH3A2CQNZZ).
On the Records tab, tick the checkbox of the row with Record name bioconductor.org and Type NS. It is the third row. Tick only that one row.
Click Edit record in the details panel on the right.
Leave Record name empty and Record type NS. Do not touch the Value box. It must still list exactly these four lines:
ns-1784.awsdns-31.co.uk.
ns-1459.awsdns-54.org.
ns-876.awsdns-45.net.
ns-91.awsdns-11.com.
In TTL (seconds), replace 172800 with 3600.
Click Save. The banner reads that the record was updated; the change status goes from PENDING to INSYNC within about a minute.
Check from a terminal — the second column must read 3600:
dig +norec +noall +answer @ns-1784.awsdns-31.co.uk bioconductor.org NS
Note the time. Step 2b should start 48 hours later, when the last 172800-second cache entries have expired. If it slips, nothing breaks: the switch just has a longer tail, and it doesn’t change how fast a rollback is.

Equivalent with the AWS CLI, for anyone with a profile in that account:
aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z2LMJH3A2CQNZZ \
  --change-batch '{"Changes":[{"Action":"UPSERT","ResourceRecordSet":{
    "Name":"bioconductor.org.","Type":"NS","TTL":3600,"ResourceRecords":[
      {"Value":"ns-1784.awsdns-31.co.uk."},{"Value":"ns-1459.awsdns-54.org."},
      {"Value":"ns-876.awsdns-45.net."},{"Value":"ns-91.awsdns-11.com."}]}}]}'
Undo: the same edit with 172800. Nothing else in the zone needs a TTL change: apex and www are already 300 s in the Cloudflare copy.
From here until two weeks after 2b: record freeze. Any change to the zone is made in both Route53 and Cloudflare, or not at all — the rollback depends on Route53 being right.


2b. Switch

Re-verify on the day. The zone must not have drifted since the copy:
./dns/verify-zone.sh | tail -1        # must print "== 0 differing record(s)"
B=will.ns.cloudflare.com ./dns/verify-zone.sh | tail -1
Also confirm the Route53 console still says Records (152). The script only checks names in the index, so a record added in Route53 since 2026-09-28 shows up as a count mismatch, not a diff — add it to Cloudflare and the index first.
Copy the two nameservers from the Cloudflare dashboard (bioconductor.org → Overview). Copy them; do not type them.
AWS console → Route 53 → Registered domains → bioconductor.org → Actions → Edit name servers. Replace the four awsdns entries with brynne.ns.cloudflare.com and will.ns.cloudflare.com (only those two). Save. Do not transfer the registration, and do not turn on DNSSEC.
Watch the parent:
dig +short NS bioconductor.org @$(dig +short NS org. | head -1)
It shows the Cloudflare pair within minutes. Then click Check nameservers now on the Cloudflare Overview page. The zone turns Active, and Cloudflare sends an email, within minutes to a few hours.
Post-checks once Active:

A=1.1.1.1 ./dns/verify-zone.sh and A=8.8.8.8 ./dns/verify-zone.sh — the public view against Cloudflare, expect 0.
curl -sI https://bioconductor.org/ | grep -i via still shows CloudFront.
Send a message to and from a @bioconductor.org address (forwardemail), and check a Brevo send.
ssh -T git@git.bioconductor.org still reaches gitolite.
Spot-check a GitHub Pages site (blog.) and a Netlify one (bioc2026.).


Rollback: Registered domains → bioconductor.org → Actions → Edit name servers → put back exactly:
ns-1784.awsdns-31.co.uk
ns-1459.awsdns-54.org
ns-876.awsdns-45.net
ns-91.awsdns-11.com
Most resolvers move back within the parent’s 1 hour. Cloudflare’s own NS records carry 86400 s (not adjustable on this plan), so a few resolvers keep asking Cloudflare for up to a day. That is harmless only if the Cloudflare zone keeps serving the same data. On rollback, leave the Cloudflare zone in place and unchanged for at least two days before deleting or editing it.
Only roll back the nameservers when Cloudflare’s DNS service is the problem. A wrong or missing record is faster to fix in Cloudflare itself (records carry 300 s TTLs), and every resolver sees the fix, including the ones a rollback would leave behind.
Afterwards: leave the Route53 hosted zone untouched for at least two weeks (it’s the rollback target), then lift the freeze. Enable DNSSEC in Cloudflare only after that, as its own change.



3. Flip the site (M1 proper)
Mechanism: a Workers route plus the proxy toggle, not a Workers Custom Domain.

A route (bioconductor.org/* → bioc-site) only intercepts traffic on proxied records. It can be deployed days ahead and sits inert while apex and www are DNS only.
The flip is switching those two records to Proxied. The rollback is switching them back to DNS only. At that point traffic goes straight to CloudFront again, because the CNAME to the CloudFront distribution never changed. That’s two clicks, with no deploy and no record deletion.
A Custom Domain needs the existing record deleted, then recreates and owns it itself. The rollback target would be gone and would have to be retyped under pressure.
The routes go in worker/wrangler.jsonc in bioc-edge (then bioc-cloudflare), not the dashboard. wrangler deploy replaces a Worker’s routes with the config’s, so a dashboard-only route disappears on the next deploy.

Before the flip:

Edge certificate. After the zone goes Active: SSL/TLS → Edge Certificates must show the Universal certificate (bioconductor.org, *.bioconductor.org) as Active. Proxying before it is Active serves TLS errors. Set SSL/TLS mode to Full (strict); CloudFront holds a valid certificate for the names, so any request the Worker passes to origin still verifies.
Logging (ADR 0003): the Worker’s Logpush job is delivering, and a record-count alert exists. Once traffic moves, CloudFront logs stop accruing.
Plain HTTP. Decide whether to turn Always Use HTTPS on (it matches production’s 301). It only affects proxied names.
Rehearse on a spare name. Add next.bioconductor.org CNAME → bioconductor.org, Proxied, plus a route next.bioconductor.org/*. Run cutover-diff.sh (bioc-edge; then bioc-cloudflare) against it. This catches any place the Worker assumes the dev hostname.
Deploy the routes (inert until proxied). In worker/wrangler.jsonc:
"routes": [
  { "pattern": "bioc-dev.cancerdatasci.org", "custom_domain": true },
  { "pattern": "bioconductor.org/*",     "zone_name": "bioconductor.org" },
  { "pattern": "www.bioconductor.org/*", "zone_name": "bioconductor.org" }
]
Confirm under Workers Routes in the zone that both appear.

Flip: DNS → Records. On the bioconductor.org CNAME, click Edit, switch Proxy status on, and Save. Repeat for www.
Verify: - curl -sI https://bioconductor.org/ and https://www.bioconductor.org/ show server: cloudflare and no via: … cloudfront. - Run cutover-diff.sh against production. - Watch Workers → bioc-site → Metrics for errors, and the Logpush destination for records.
Rollback: the same two records, Proxy status off, then Save. Resolvers holding Cloudflare’s addresses expire within 300 s. Leave the routes deployed; they are inert again. Keep CloudFront and master running until M2 retires them.


Found along the way — fix separately, not during the move

The spreadsheet lists a TXT record on a literal @.bioconductor.org label carrying v=spf1 include:spf.forwardemail.net -all. It is a data-entry mistake for the apex. Route53 serves it at that literal name, and Cloudflare refuses the name. The apex has no SPF record at all (checked 2026-09-28). Its TXT records are only acevhogcbpv6dssaq15fbe1ek8, a Brevo code and a forwardemail verification, and the include:_spf.mlsend.com SPF seen in the 2026-09 review is gone. With _dmarc at p=reject, mail from the domain now depends on DKIM alignment alone. Add a real apex SPF (forwardemail + Brevo + SES) as its own change, in both zones during the freeze.
The apex TXT value acevhogcbpv6dssaq15fbe1ek8 has no recorded owner.
testweb is an Alias to a CloudFront distribution that no longer exists — delete it from Route53.
bbr/*.bbr still carry a Route53 health-checked failover to an AKS address. Delete them, along with the health checks (which bill monthly).
Since the 2026-09 review, several delete candidates are already gone (tokay*, merida*, malbec*, machv2, celaya2, monitor, docbuilder, kjohnson1, meet). New since then: autoconfig/autodiscover (forwardemail), status, testgalaxy, eurobioc2027, the Brevo DKIM selectors. Many A-record targets also moved (e.g. workshop is now 149.165.152.155). The per-host detail below predates this and is not re-probed.

title: Data and workflow packages in r-universe: a size audit
text:
NoteA dated measurement, not a live view



Numbers are from 2026-09-02 against Bioconductor 3.23 (release, R 4.6). Package sizes move every release; the script that produced these figures is package-sizes.py in this repository, so they can be regenerated rather than trusted.
r-universe-org/sync#8 proposes adding Bioconductor’s data-experiment and workflow packages to the bioc and bioc-release universes, which today carry software packages only. Jeroen Ooms objected on size grounds: r-universe enforces a 100 MB limit on source and binary packages, some data packages exceed 1 GB, and every added package gets binaries and checks built for every platform — “costly duplication” for data that does not change.
That objection is correct in direction. It has not been correct in magnitude, in either direction, because nobody had measured the corpus. This page measures it. What the limit precisely is, where it is enforced, and how it relates to GitHub’s and Bioconductor’s own size rules is a separate question, answered in Size limits in the r-universe build — in short, it is 100 MiB rather than 100 MB, it applies independently to the source package and to each binary, and it is r-universe’s own policy rather than a GitHub constraint.

title: Data and workflow packages in r-universe: a size audit
text:
What r-universe actually ingests
The cost argument depends on the pipeline, so it is worth being precise about it. r-universe does not consume Bioconductor’s built tarballs. The sync action builds a registry of git URLs, clones each one, and builds from source:





flowchart LR
  G["git.bioconductor.org<br/>/packages/<pkg>"] -->|"mirror"| M["github.com/bioc/<pkg><br/>3,770 repos"]
  M -->|"registry entry<br/>(sync/R/monorepos.R)"| R["monorepo submodule"]
  R -->|"R CMD build"| S["source package<br/>(100 MB gate)"]
  S -->|"per platform<br/>× R version"| B["8–14 binary artifacts<br/>linux · mac · win · wasm"]

  classDef ok fill:#f3fbf4,stroke:#3d8b47,color:#12263f
  classDef gate fill:#fff8e6,stroke:#b8860b,color:#12263f
  class G,M,R,B ok
  class S gate






Two consequences follow, and both matter more than the headline tarball sizes.
First, the gate is the git mirror, not the tarball. monorepos.R already carries a hand-maintained escape hatch for this — nomirror <- c('SwathXtend', 'h5vc', 'scafari', 'singIST'), commented “large git files” — which routes four software packages straight at git.bioconductor.org because GitHub will not take them. Everything else is assumed to be on the mirror.
Second, storage is multiplied, not added. Sampling the live bioc universe API, packages carry 8 to 14 binary artifacts each (SummarizedExperiment and GenomicRanges: 8; limma and S4Vectors: 14) across linux, macOS, Windows and wasm targets crossed with R versions.
For data packages that multiplier applies almost in full. Unpacking four experiment tarballs, 96–100% of their bytes sit in data/ and inst/ — precisely the directories R CMD INSTALL preserves:

section: Finding 5: the data do not change
text:
Finding 5: the data do not change
Jeroen’s framing question — “I thought that data were fixed and do not need the continuous checks/binaries?” — turns out to be answerable from the mirror.
Bioconductor mirrors keep several release versions of each tarball side by side. Comparing each experiment package’s current tarball against its immediately preceding release:




Packages
Share

And of the 67 packages over the 100 MB limit — the ones whose rebuild costs the most — 67 of 67 were stable across the bump. The expensive packages are precisely the inert ones.
Tarball size is a proxy for content, not proof of it: a version-string change in DESCRIPTION moves a few bytes, and gzip output shifts with timestamps. But at 98% the signal is not ambiguous. The version numbers advance every release because Bioconductor bumps every package every release, not because the data changed.
This reframes the cost question. It is not “is 28 GiB affordable” but “is rebuilding an unchanged 3 GiB tarball into 8 binaries twice a year a thing worth building at all.”

The 74 excluded packages are not a rounding error either. They include most of what makes the experiment repo worth having: curatedOvarianData, curatedCRCData, RTCGA.*, the FlowSorted.* reference panels, msdata. A merge that lands 84% of the packages and drops the large curated datasets delivers the discoverability benefit unevenly, in a way that is invisible from the universe page.

title: Data and workflow packages in r-universe: a size audit
text:
What this suggests
Stated as options rather than a recommendation — the decision is r-universe’s and Bioconductor’s, not this repository’s.

Split the PR. Workflows are 100 MiB and 24 packages and have essentially none of the objected-to properties. They can merge on their own merits today, minus methylationArrayAnalysis. Experiment data is a genuinely different question.
Fix the registry to skip what it cannot fetch. Whatever else is decided, generating URLs for 31 repos that do not exist is a defect. The check is one API call per package against the mirror org, or a nomirror-style list — but the list is 74 long, which argues for computing it.
Screen on git size, not tarball size. Finding 4 shows the two are uncorrelated for this corpus. depmap passes the wrong test and fails the right one.
Register data packages without building them. The value being sought is discoverability — landing pages, search, dependency graphs — and Finding 5 says the builds and checks produce no new information. If r-universe can carry a package as metadata plus a pointer to Bioconductor’s existing tarball, the objection largely dissolves. This is a feature request, not a configuration.
Take the ORAS/registry suggestion seriously for the tail. 11 packages hold 34% of the bytes. Bioconductor already splits large data out of source control — every experiment tarball carries an external_data_store.txt listing the directories (data, inst/extdata) the build system stores externally and re-attaches at build time. The mechanism exists; the question is whether r-universe can read from it.

Note also the scope boundary: data-annotation is not in this PR, and it is 89.12 GiB across 928 packages with 126 over the limit and 9 over 1 GiB. Only 50 of the 928 are mirrored at all. Whatever is decided for experiment data will be asked about annotation next, and the answer cannot be the same one.

title: Data and workflow packages in r-universe: a size audit
text:
Method
package-sizes.py in this repository reproduces every number above. It:

Reads PACKAGES.gz from bioconductor.org/packages/release/<repo>/src/contrib/ for bioc, data/experiment, data/annotation, workflows and books to get the authoritative package/version list for BioC 3.23 (3,784 packages).
Reads exact byte sizes from a Bioconductor mirror’s Apache directory index (ftp.gwdg.de/pub/misc/bioconductor) — one request per repo rather than 3,784 HEAD requests against bioconductor.org, which rate-limits. All 3,784 current versions matched.
Enumerates all 3,770 repos in github.com/bioc via the GitHub API for git mirror sizes and mirror coverage.
Compares each package’s current tarball size against its previous release version, both present in the mirror index, for the churn figures.
Samples bioc.r-universe.dev/api/packages/<pkg> for binary artifact counts.

Caveats worth carrying:

Sizes are Bioconductor’s tarballs, not r-universe’s. r-universe runs its own R CMD build from git, and the results differ — TCGAbiolinks is 63.8 MiB on bioconductor.org and 30.5 MiB in the universe. The 100 MB gate applies to r-universe’s artifact. Packages near the line may fall either side of it.
The 100 MB figure is quoted from the PR comment, not read out of r-universe’s source.
Binary sizes are estimated, not measured: Bioconductor publishes binaries for software only (data/experiment/bin/** is empty and 404s on bioconductor.org), so there is no observed data-package binary to weigh. The estimate rests on the tar composition above.
Churn is inferred from tarball size, as noted in Finding 5.
Mirror coverage is a snapshot. Repos can be added; 30 missing today is not 30 missing forever.

title: Cloudflare Account Migration
text:
NoteStatus: plan, deferred



The bioconductor.org zone went into the current Cloudflare account (the personal account 55bf7202…, which already holds the bioc-site Worker, Workers Paid and R2 Paid) so the DNS cutover did not wait on an account move. See the DNS cutover runbook. This page is the plan for moving everything to a dedicated Bioconductor account after the cutover has settled. It has not been rehearsed, and items marked verify have not been confirmed against Cloudflare.

title: Cloudflare Account Migration
text:
Why move
The Worker, R2 buckets, dev hostname and now the production zone share an account with unrelated personal domains.

Permissions are account-wide. Workers and R2 rights can’t be scoped to one project, so a Bioconductor co-admin would hold rights over unrelated infrastructure, and the reverse.
Billing, grants and sponsorships attach to an account. Bioconductor’s bill should not be one person’s card.
Bus factor. A project account with 2–3 super administrators survives any one person leaving. A personal account doesn’t.

title: Cloudflare Account Migration
section: What it costs to do later instead of first
text:
What it costs to do later instead of first
Doing it after the cutover means a second nameserver change on the live production  domain. A zone can’t be handed between accounts. It’s added fresh to the new account, which assigns different nameservers, and the registrar is repointed. That is the price of not blocking the cutover. It’s manageable because the zone is small, fully scripted, and the procedure below keeps both accounts serving identical answers throughout.

title: Cloudflare Account Migration
text:
Inventory — what moves, and how
It’s a redeploy, not a rebuild. Everything except data is declared in wrangler.jsonc.
