~143 GB



Roughly 550–600 GB compressed across ~800,000 objects, all flat at the bucket root.
Parquet lands at roughly parity with the gzipped source. Measured on two full months, mirroring every row and every column: June 2026 gave 157,956,840 rows in 437 seconds, July 2026 gave 175,314,722 rows in 553 seconds and 12 GB. Columnar zstd on highly repetitive log fields compresses about as well as gzip does row-wise, so keeping everything costs far less than a row count suggests — the whole archive projects to 550–600 GB and 8–10 hours, and it parallelizes by month.

Mirror the logs; interpret them locally
DuckDB reads the gzipped logs straight out of S3 with a glob, so there is no need to stage a copy as a processing step. More importantly, nothing should be filtered on the way in — neither columns nor rows.
That is the specific mistake to avoid, because both existing pipelines made it, and made it twice. Each projects down to a handful of columns at ingest, discarding cs(User-Agent) and x-forwarded-for, which is precisely why neither can filter bots or handle proxied clients today. Each also filters to package-tarball requests at ingest, which discards about 97% of the log — every content page, every vignette, every crawler hitting documentation. The columns and rows were never missing from the source; they were thrown away upstream, and recovering them means re-reading six years from S3.
Filtering at ingest also bakes in the very policies under dispute — whether redirects count, whether 206 counts, whether HEAD counts. Those become unaskable. So the mirror stays raw and the download definition lives in a view over it. The egress is paid once; what is kept afterwards is free.
This matters beyond download statistics. A complete mirror supports questions the published series cannot touch at all: user journeys through the site, which of the hundreds of thousands of content pages carry value, and bot pressure against documentation rather than against tarballs.
A full rclone copy of the original gzip is still worth doing, but as a backup rather than a pipeline stage: the bucket is currently the only copy of the 2020-onward raw logs, with no versioning or lifecycle protection in evidence. A Parquet mirror is a derived artifact and depends on the column mapping being right; a byte-identical copy does not.


The script
cloudfront-logs-to-parquet.py in the working repository behind this site does the mirroring: one Parquet file per month, Hive-partitioned as year=YYYY/month=M/, so the result queries as a single table with pruning on either level.
A month at a time rather than a day gives ~80 files of tens of megabytes instead of ~2,400 of around one — fewer, larger row groups compress better and query faster. Two partition levels rather than a single month=YYYY-MM allows pruning by year alone, and matches the year=/month=/day= layout Bioconductor already used for its own abandoned Parquet extract. date and time are kept in the data rather than merely implied by the partition, because the question this exists to settle is a month-boundary dispute — day- and hour-level detail across that boundary is the one thing that must not be aggregated away.
The mirror copies and does not interpret: every row, all 33 fields, VARCHAR exactly as logged apart from date. The download definition — package tarball or binary under /packages/, status in 200/301/302/307/308, HEAD excluded — lives in a DOWNLOADS_SQL view, so its output stays directly comparable to what the two series publish while remaining a policy that can be changed without re-reading anything. It deliberately does not filter bots; the point is to preserve that decision for the team rather than pre-empt it.
The view is the part that can drift, so the script carries a --self-check that exercises it against known-good and known-bad URLs (tarball, Windows binary, annotation package, redirect, 404, partial content, HEAD, an HTML page, a PACKAGES index). It also asserts that the mirror stays a mirror — the check fails if the copy grows a WHERE clause or a derived column.
Two guards matter more than they look. The column mapping is positional, and the reader skips the #Fields: header, so an upstream format change would silently shift every column; the script verifies the field count per month and refuses to continue on a mismatch. The header was checked byte-for-byte at 2020, 2023 and 2026 and is identical, but the assertion is what keeps that true.
Against the mirrored months, cs_user_agent alone separates libcurl, RStudio, R, Wget, renv and browser traffic — the distinction neither published series can currently draw.
The rebuild answered the open question, and the answer was not the expected one. Recomputing June and July 2026 showed both published series undercounting for unrelated reasons; the numbers are in Resolved: both published series undercount. Validation came out clean along the way: the mirror reproduces published 2020 figures to within 0.15%, and July 2026 distinct IPs to within 0.008%.

title: Download Stats
section: What this means for the migration
text:
What this means for the migration






ImportantThe R2 migration removes this pipeline’s only input



Both systems are fed exclusively by CloudFront access logs. Serving package downloads from Cloudflare instead of CloudFront stops those logs being produced — and with the Squid and Apache ingests already commented out, there is no second source to fall back on. Download statistics stop accruing on the day traffic moves, for both systems at once, whatever else has been migrated.
Cloudflare can emit equivalent logs, but nothing reads them today and the field layout differs from the CloudFront W3C format the Athena table and the legacy parsers both assume. This is a prerequisite for the traffic cutover, not a follow-up.



What replaces the logs






TipThis is no longer a proposal — the replacement is live (2026-08-13)



The design below is implemented and running. The Worker has been emitting one full record per request since early August; the record uses the CloudFront field vocabulary, so the two eras line up column-for-column. Logpush delivers continuously to durable object storage (the destination moved from R2 to Google Cloud Storage on 2026-08-10, for isolation of logging output from operational data), external tables make both eras queryable in one place, and a single normalizing view presents the Cloudflare records with the identical columns, names and types as the CloudFront archive — cross-era statistics are a plain UNION ALL, verified. Delivery is gap-alerted daily through the same failure channel as the sync jobs, because Logpush cannot backfill and a silent gap is permanent loss. The CloudFront side still accrues in parallel, so the deliberate cutover overlap this page calls for is already underway. The prerequisite in the callout above is met.


Cloudflare’s Logpush HTTP requests dataset is Enterprise-only, and Bioconductor is not on Enterprise. That rules out the direct analogue of CloudFront-to-S3 and settles the design:

Worker emits one structured JSON record per request via console.log, shipped by Workers Trace Events Logpush to object storage. Trace Events Logpush is available on the Workers Paid plan, and the 16,384-character limit on the combined logs field is ample for a single record. The Worker is already in the request path, so this needs no additional infrastructure.
Tail Workers consume the same event stream with code in the middle. Reach for one only if the record needs shaping Logpush cannot express — not as the system of record. The documentation does not state delivery guarantees, sampling under load, or overload behaviour, and they bill on CPU time, which at this request volume is a real per-request cost Logpush does not carry.
Workers Analytics Engine retains data for three months. That makes it a live dashboard, never the record behind a series reaching back to 2009.

Three constraints carry over from everything above. Take all fields and no sampling — Logpush offers both knobs, and using them is the same mistake that left both current pipelines unable to filter bots. Monitor the push: Logpush cannot backfill, so a failed or disabled job is permanent loss, and the failure is silent. Overlap the cutover deliberately — run CloudFront and Cloudflare logging together for at least a month, because the only reason anything on this page could be validated is that two pipelines happened to overlap by accident.
Field names differ between the two (ClientIP against c-ip, EdgeResponseStatus against sc-status). Normalising at ingest would repeat the mistake; keep the eras in separate partitions and put a normalising view on top.

/packages/stats/ is a dynamic application, not files. Everything else this repository proposes to move to R2 is static content. This is a Flask app over a Postgres database, reached through a proxy rule in master’s Apache. A Worker serving objects from R2 cannot replace it — it needs somewhere to keep running, and a route pointing at it.
It is the last thing keeping that proxy rule alive, alongside Solr. Both need a destination before master’s Apache can be retired.
The raw logs are recoverable, contrary to the design notes. Those notes say objects in the CloudFront log bucket are destroyed after six months. Measured, that is not what happens: the oldest object present is dated 2020-01-01 and every year since is represented, so roughly 6.6 years are retained with no lifecycle expiry in evidence. Statistics from 2020 onward could therefore be recomputed from source if either database were lost — which makes a rebuild a viable answer to the June/July discrepancy, rather than something to be patched forward. This applies only from 2020; everything earlier has no surviving raw source and is irreplaceable. Two caveats: continuous delivery only starts in January 2024 (2020–2023 objects were bulk-loaded in November 2023, so their completeness is unverified), and the bucket has no prefix structure at all — every object sits flat at the root, which is why a full listing takes minutes and why the Athena table scans everything.
Neither system has working CI. The current repository’s only workflow is bound to branch names that do not exist in it, and has never run. There are no tests over the ingestion path in either system.
The current repository has an open issue reporting a hardcoded Flask secret key committed to version control. It is unresolved on the default branch and should be handled before this application is redeployed anywhere.
Raw client IP addresses are retained indefinitely, both in the source logs going back to 2020 and as a column in the downloads table. The system’s own design notes proposed encrypting them; that was not implemented. Anything that moves or copies this database is moving personal data, and is worth a deliberate decision rather than an inherited default.

title: Download Stats
text:
What could not be determined

Which specific days the current system lost in June 2026. The shortfall is 2,207,644 downloads distributed through the month, but the published tables are monthly only, so the affected days cannot be identified from outside — it needs a query against the downloads table.
Whether the packages-table refresh runs anywhere. It is not in the repository’s cron script, but a manual or externally scheduled invocation would not be visible from the repository.
Whether the legacy VM’s actual crontab matches its README, which is the only description of it. Nothing was logged into to check.
Whether either system’s database is backed up. Given that the 2009–2019 statistics exist nowhere else, this is the most consequential unknown on the page.
The exact last year covered by the 2023 database import. The script covers 2009–2020, a commit message claims “through 2022”, and the measured agreement suggests at least 2021. Settling it needs a query against the downloads table.
Whether the 2020–2023 portion of the log archive is complete. Those objects were bulk-loaded in one pass in November 2023; only continuous delivery from January 2024 onward is self-evidently complete.
Whether anyone is monitoring the divergence. Both systems publish; only one is linked.

title: What the new site has changed
text:
NoteA running record



These are the stories of what moving bioconductor.org onto the new stack has made better, and what it has made possible that wasn’t before. Each one says how far along it is. Some are done and measured, some are measured but not yet realized, and some are just started. Where a number is a projection rather than a measurement, it says so. New stories go at the top.
crumbs: What the New Site Has Changed

title: What the new site has changed
section: Watching the logs caught a crawler eating three quarters of the site
text:
Watching the logs caught a crawler eating three quarters of the site
Status: fixed 2026-09-28, the same evening: the loop broken at 20:58 UTC, the rest of the crawler blocked at the edge at 22:34 UTC (bioc-edge#32). The daily savings are still projected from minutes of data.
bioconductor.org moved onto the new edge on the afternoon of 2026-09-28. Within the hour we were reading the request logs, which the new edge writes one structured record per request, and one thing stood out immediately. In the first 19 minutes, 84,414 of 112,632 requests (75%) came from a single crawler. It ran on two cloud-hosting networks in Singapore, spread across 1,130 addresses, and rotated three Mac Chrome user agents so it looked like ordinary browsers.
It was requesting paths like /talks/2016/BioC2016/ConcurrentWorkshops1/Sauteraud/2016/..., up to 294 characters long, and the reason is a loop we were feeding. The old site redirects anything under /talks to the course-materials index, and the new edge copied that rule. The index has 392 relative links, such as 2022/CSAMA/. The crawler resolved them against the address it had asked for instead of the page it landed on, so every redirect produced 392 new /talks/... addresses, each of which redirected back to the same index. The redirect never helped a person either. It discarded the rest of the path, so an old link to a talk landed on a list of every talk, and in the logs nobody but the crawler asked for /talks.
We removed the rule, so those paths now return 404, and wrote the general policy down as ADR 0013: keep redirects that land a reader on the page they wanted, keep anything package clients depend on, and drop catch-alls to index pages. In the first minutes after the change, the crawler’s fetches of the course-materials page went from 41,873 to zero and its request rate fell from about 8,300 to about 3,400 a minute. What remained was the crawler working through addresses it had already queued, and we expected that to run dry, since a 404 page gives it nothing new.
It didn’t. The loop had given the crawler an enormous queue, and it kept working through it at about 3,700 requests a minute, still well over half of everything the site received. Worse, each of those 404s now cost the edge a few storage lookups, where the redirects had cost none. Caching 404s helped every other client but not this one, because every address it asked for was new. So we added one firewall rule in Cloudflare, scoped as narrowly as we could make it: requests from those two networks, and only for paths under /talks/, are blocked before they reach our code. The site has nothing under /talks/, so no real content can be caught by it, and the same networks’ other requests still get through. It blocked 7,500 requests in its first few minutes. The crawler’s traffic reaching the site went from 5,000 to 8,000 requests a minute to between none and fifteen, and blocked requests cost us nothing: no compute, no storage reads, no log volume. Without request-level logs we would have seen a busy site, not one crawler, and blocking whole cloud networks to stop it would have caught real users too.
The old site almost certainly had the same crawler, since production has the identical rule. We couldn’t see it: the old logs fed statistics jobs, and nobody was reading them request by request. The same afternoon’s logs turned up two smaller problems, which were fixed the same day. 774 requests for old links with a doubled slash (/packages//release/...) got a 404 where the old server quietly served the page. A download resuming past the end of a file got an error instead of the right “nothing left to send” answer.
Taken together, that is somewhere between 5 and 12 million fewer requests a day, depending on which stretch of the first evening you take as the crawler’s normal rate: well over half of the edge’s request and log volume. Those figures are projected from minutes of data, and a full day’s comparison will replace them.
crumbs: What the New Site Has Changed

title: What the new site has changed
section: Costs: about $5,000 a month down to a couple of hundred
text:
Costs: about $5,000 a month down to a couple of hundred
Status: projected, and re-estimated 2026-09-28 from the first hours of production traffic. The Cloudflare side is running now; the AWS side retires at milestone M2, so today we pay for both. Prices are Cloudflare’s published list prices, not a bill.
The legacy estate costs about $5,000 a month in AWS: CloudFront, the S3 bucket, and the master and staging web servers. That is before the builder hardware and the staff time to keep three operating systems patched. The difference is mostly egress. A package repository’s job is sending tarballs to the world, which is exactly what a CDN usually bills for most, and R2 doesn’t charge for it.
We used to quote about $80 a month for the replacement. That is the storage alone: the bucket holds 5.1 TB in 4.2 million objects, about $77 a month. Serving traffic adds per-request charges on top, and the first hours in production let us estimate them from real numbers instead of guessing. At today’s rate of about 6.8 million requests a day, with the crawler from the story above still working through its queue, the whole stack comes to roughly $500 a month. Most of that is R2 reads, about 800 million a month, and the crawler causes most of those: its 404s each cost a few storage lookups. Without the crawler it is roughly $240 a month. Caching 404s, which are now the largest source of storage reads, should bring it to around $170, still falling as the edge caches fill. So the honest figure is a couple of hundred dollars a month, not $80, against $5,000. The overview has the AWS breakdown.
Since 2026-10-02 we also record what both providers actually bill, day by day, so this story can move from projections to measured costs over time. A daily job collects the Bioconductor AWS account’s costs from Cost Explorer, back to 2025-09-01, and the Cloudflare account’s usage charges, back to 2026-06-17, which is as far as Cloudflare’s billing API goes. The Cloudflare account also hosts unrelated projects, so its figures are an upper bound for Bioconductor. The code is in the private infra-costs repository.
crumbs: What the New Site Has Changed

title: What the new site has changed
section: Faster, smaller downloads, and a regression we caught
text:
Faster, smaller downloads, and a regression we caught
Status: measured 2026-09-28 from one well-connected host in Denver, before and after fixing the regression described below.
The old site answers only over HTTP/1.1. The July 2026 performance audit measured an 11-second first paint on the homepage over a slow mobile connection, mostly from fetching dozens of small files one after another over a handful of connections. The new edge speaks HTTP/2 and compresses everything it serves, including the repository indexes that every install.packages() call reads, which the old site sends uncompressed. PACKAGES for the software repository goes over the wire as 236 KB instead of 944 KB, and VIEWS as 1.2 MB instead of 5.3 MB, about a quarter of the size each time. That matters most for exactly the people the audit worried about: users on slow or metered connections.
The same measurement found a regression, and it’s fixed. Package files (tarballs, PACKAGES, VIEWS, config.yaml) were never being served from the edge cache: a rule that protects newly built pages from stale copies had ended up covering the whole site, so every package download went back to storage. bioc-edge#36, the fix for #35, let the cache lookup include files only the mirror can hold, and those files now come from the edge cache, still expiring as soon as a package changes. From Denver, PACKAGES went from 447 to 85 ms, VIEWS from 550 to 205 ms, a tarball from 227 to 72 ms and config.yaml, which BiocManager reads on every call, from 232 to 58 ms. CloudFront is still faster from this one host, by 30 to 50 ms. About a third of that is network distance from this particular machine, and the rest is time spent in the Worker on every request, cached or not. That gap is the next thing to look at.
crumbs: What the New Site Has Changed

title: What the new site has changed
section: Download statistics that can tell people from bots
text:
Download statistics that can tell people from bots
Status: in progress. The logs are being collected now. The classification is bioc-traffic#5: a first version (v0) is written and in use for analysis, and the issue is still open on 2026-10-01. bioc-registry#26 tracks generating statistics from the de-identified access log; it leaves the definition of a download to the classification. Published statistics still come from the legacy pipelines.
Bioconductor’s download statistics have never filtered bots. The legacy code has a list of known crawlers and build-node addresses, and the checks that use them are commented out; the newer system never reads the user agent at all. The download statistics page shows what that costs. In August and September 2025, downloads roughly quadrupled while the number of distinct clients didn’t move: CI and container builds reinstalling the same base packages. Those two months are still inflated in every published table and in the ranking behind each package’s Rank. Separately, a quarter of June 2026 went missing from the published series without anyone noticing.
The new edge keeps every request, with fields that help tell traffic apart: the client’s network (ASN), Cloudflare’s category for verified bots, and hashes of the TLS client hello. It has no bot score and no JA4 fingerprint; those need Cloudflare’s Enterprise Bot Management. The crawler above is a good example of why the network field matters. Its user agents claim to be browsers, so a user-agent filter would have counted it as people; its two networks give it away. The plan is a classification we build and maintain ourselves, with versioned rules so history can be recomputed when they change, and statistics generated from it as static files. Web usage and package usage are reported separately, rather than as one number that mixes people, installs and crawlers.
crumbs: What the New Site Has Changed

title: What the new site has changed
section: The build system migration has a path forward
text:
The build system migration has a path forward
Status: early. A working proof of concept in bioc-build, with a handful of successful builds as of early September 2026.
The move off the legacy build machines stalled on one gap: r-universe builds Bioconductor’s software packages, but not the experiment-data and workflow packages. Some are far bigger than its size limit, and until something else builds them, the old machines can’t be turned off. We measured that corpus instead of guessing at it. It is 434 experiment-data packages totalling 28 GiB, with 67 of them holding three quarters of the bytes, and 25 workflow packages that together fit in 319 MiB. The data almost never change: across the last release bump, 425 of 433 experiment packages shipped a tarball whose size moved by less than 1%.
bioc-build is a build pipeline on GitHub Actions that starts from a pinned copy of r-universe’s own workflow and diverges only where it has to: a configurable size limit, packages authorized by a reviewed manifest, and dependencies resolved from the new registry. Staying that close to r-universe means a package both systems build should produce the same artifact and the same check result, which is what makes a comparison possible. It is early, but the part that was stuck now has a route.
crumbs: What the New Site Has Changed

title: Installing packages
text:
Since 2026-09-28, bioconductor.org is served by the new stack: a Cloudflare Worker in front of a copy of the full repository in R2 (see the overview for the design). There is nothing to change on your side. BiocManager::install() reads the same URLs it always has, and gets the same packages, tarballs and checksums, because the new stack still copies the legacy build output from master.bioconductor.org hourly, and a weekly job checksums R2 against that local copy.
Checked on the day of the switch: BiocManager::install() against bioconductor.org passes for release (3.23) and devel (3.24), from reading config.yaml through PACKAGES to installing and loading a package.

title: Installing packages
section: Is my install coming from the new stack?
text:
Is my install coming from the new stack?
Any response from bioconductor.org now carries server: cloudflare and no via: … cloudfront header:
curl -sI https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/src/contrib/PACKAGES | grep -i -e '^server' -e '^via'

title: Installing packages
text:
What to expect

Same URLs, same content. Landing pages, vignettes, archives and old releases all live at the addresses they always had. Two exceptions: /talks/ pages return 404 (ADR 0013), and site search (/solr) is not served.
Smaller downloads. Everything is compressed, including the repository indexes R reads on every install: PACKAGES goes over the wire at about a quarter of its size.
Package updates appear within about an hour of being published, as before. “Published” means built by the Bioconductor Build System (BBS) and propagated to master.bioconductor.org, not pushed to git.bioconductor.org. A URL requested just before a file appears can 404 for up to ten minutes more (see edge cache).

title: Installing packages
text:
Reporting problems
An install that fails, a checksum mismatch, a slow or missing file, a page that renders wrong: all worth reporting, however small. Use one of the bioc-infrastructure issue forms, package install problem or something’s broken on bioconductor.org, with the R output and, if possible, the failing URL. Reports are triaged by hand and moved to the repo that owns the problem (how reporting works). You can also email Sean Davis (seandavi@gmail.com).

title: Running a Bioconductor mirror
text:
This replaces the rsync-over-SSH instructions at bioconductor.org/about/mirrors/mirror-how-to/. Those instructions depend on master.bioconductor.org, which milestone M2 retires. The new site has no rsync server. Instead it publishes a manifest: a list of every object in the package repositories, with sizes and MD5s, that any HTTP client can sync from.
No credentials, no sign-up form, no SSH key. Fetch the manifest, fetch the files, recreate the symlinks, serve the tree.

title: Running a Bioconductor mirror
text:
What changed









Old
New




Source
bioc-rsync@master.bioconductor.org over SSH
https://bioconductor.org/api/v1/manifest/index.json over HTTPS


Access
SSH key, requested by form
none


Tool
rsync -zrtlv --delete
rclone copy --files-from


Symlinks
created by hand: release and devel
listed in the manifest index (202 on 2026-09-30); the script recreates release, devel and the R-version aliases


Current version numbers
in the rsync module names
in index.json, read every run


Cadence
release monthly-ish, devel at most weekly
manifest regenerated on every hourly sync; syncing daily is enough

title: Running a Bioconductor mirror
text:
The manifest







Endpoint
Contents




GET /api/v1/manifest/index.json
which numeric versions release and devel point at, the symlink map, per-manifest object counts, generation timestamp


GET /api/v1/manifest/<version>/<repo>.tsv.gz
path · size · md5, one object per line, tab-separated



Repos are bioc, data-annotation, data-experiment, workflows and books, for the current release and devel only. Only the manifest names use a hyphen: the paths inside them, on the site and in your mirror are the usual packages/<version>/data/annotation/ and .../data/experiment/, so options(repos=) and R’s etc/repositories work unchanged. Older releases are not published; ask if you need them (reporting a problem).
The MD5 is a real MD5 of the object, not a composite ETag. An empty third column means no usable hash exists for that object and it should be checked by size alone. Today that column is populated for every object.

title: Running a Bioconductor mirror
text:
Choosing scope
Decide explicitly rather than mirroring everything.







Scope
Notes




bioc (src/contrib, bin/windows, bin/macosx/*)
Every mirror needs source. Binaries are comparable in size; skip if your users build from source.


data-annotation, data-experiment
Large, changes rarely.


workflows, books
Small.


Releases before the current one
Not in the manifest.


The historical archive (4.66 TB)
Not in the manifest. Never carried by any mirror.



Release and devel together are roughly 320 GB.

title: Running a Bioconductor mirror
text:
Running the sync
mirror-sync.sh is a short wrapper around rclone copy. It needs bash, curl, gunzip, jq and rclone, and checks for them before doing anything. It runs on Linux and macOS (brew install jq rclone).
curl -fsSLO https://seandavi.github.io/bioc-infrastructure/mirror-sync.sh
chmod +x mirror-sync.sh
DEST=/srv/bioc ./mirror-sync.sh          # DEST is the directory you serve as the site root
From cron, daily is plenty:
17 3 * * *  DEST=/srv/bioc /usr/local/bin/mirror-sync.sh >> /var/log/bioc-mirror-sync.log 2>&1

What it does

Reads index.json for the current release and devel versions, every run. Nothing is pinned: at a release roll the script follows the new numbers by itself.
Lists every file in those versions’ manifests for the repos you carry, then applies your INCLUDE/EXCLUDE patterns. A failed manifest download stops the run.
Copies with rclone copy --files-from. Only new and changed files are fetched, judged by size and modification time. rclone writes each file under a temporary name and renames it when complete, so your server never serves a half-written file. rclone doesn’t check the manifest’s MD5s; they’re there if you want to verify a copy yourself.
Recreates the symlinks (release, devel and the R-version aliases inside contrib/). rclone can’t make them, and without them, URLs that go through them return 404 on your mirror.

It never deletes. rclone’s http backend can’t list directories on this site, so rclone sync can’t tell “removed upstream” from “not listed” (see the warning above). Old package versions stay on disk until you remove them. At a release roll, delete the retired version yourself, e.g. rm -rf /srv/bioc/packages/3.22. That also clears the older tarballs that piled up while it was current.


Settings



Variable
Default





DEST
(required)
Directory you serve as the site root.


REPOS
bioc data-annotation data-experiment workflows books
Which repositories to carry (see Choosing scope).


INCLUDE
everything
Extended regex; copy only paths that match.


EXCLUDE
nothing
Extended regex; skip paths that match.


RCLONE_*

Any rclone setting, e.g. RCLONE_TRANSFERS=16 for more parallel downloads.



Patterns match the full path, e.g. packages/3.23/bioc/src/contrib/limma_3.66.0.tar.gz. Source packages only, no data repos:
DEST=/srv/bioc REPOS="bioc workflows books" INCLUDE='/src/contrib/' ./mirror-sync.sh
Exit status is 0 when done, and non-zero with a message on stderr otherwise. A failed run has deleted nothing; rerun it.


Without the script
The script is the recipe; you can run its steps by hand or adapt them. The part that matters is the file list:
curl -fsS https://bioconductor.org/api/v1/manifest/3.23/bioc.tsv.gz | gunzip | cut -f1 \
  | grep '/src/contrib/' > files.txt
test -s files.txt
rclone copy --http-url https://bioconductor.org :http: /srv/bioc --files-from files.txt --no-traverse
A bare rclone sync against a directory URL, the way rsync used to work, isn’t possible yet: the site serves no directory listings for rclone to read. That’s tracked in bioc-edge#61.

title: Running a Bioconductor mirror
text:
Serving
Apache and nginx serve the tree as-is. Two things to get right:

Follow symlinks. Apache needs Options +FollowSymLinks on the directory, or every release/ URL returns 403.
Do not copy .htaccess from the old origin. It redirects old-release traffic out to the archive, which would send your users away from your own mirror.

Content types come from your server’s mime.types, so extensionless files such as PACKAGES and VIEWS behave as they always have.
Users point at your mirror exactly as before:
options(BioC_mirror = "https://mirror.example.org")
BiocManager::install("GEOquery")

title: Running a Bioconductor mirror
text:
Migrating an existing rsync mirror
Point the script at the DEST you already serve and run it by hand the first time. rsync kept the old origin’s timestamps, which differ from the new site’s, so the first run may download much of the tree again; later runs fetch only what changed. If packages/release or packages/devel is a real directory rather than a symlink, move it aside first, or the script’s link lands inside it. Nothing is deleted, so files the old tree has that the manifest doesn’t stay until you remove them. Tell the Bioconductor team when you have switched, through the site problem form, so the rsync account can be closed on your say-so rather than on log silence.

title: Running a Bioconductor mirror
text:
Listing your mirror
The mirrors page and chooseBioCmirror() are still the registry. That process has not changed; the request form on the mirrors page still applies.

title: Running a Bioconductor mirror
text:
Source
The generator and the reasoning behind the design, including why read-only storage credentials and a custom client were rejected, live in the serving repo’s MIRRORS.md.

title: The propagation gate: what bioc-registry publishes, and why
text: r-universe and bioc-build build Bioconductor packages. Only some of those builds become what bioc-registry publishes: installable repositories at https://bioc-registry.seandavi.workers.dev/repo/{bioc,bioc-release}, and the propagation index that the /next/ preview pages are built from. This page states the rule that decides, read from the code that runs it.

title: The propagation gate: what bioc-registry publishes, and why
text:
The gate, check by check
Since ADR 0011 (2026-09-04) there is one decision function, gate() in src/repo.ts, with three callers and no gating anywhere else:



Caller
Producer
Config




evaluate() in src/index.ts, on every r-universe wave
r-universe
gating R from config.yaml, replace_seed: false


POST /publish (maintenance key required)
bioc-build
the R version bioc-build’s image ships, replace_seed: true, plus manifest rules


POST /gate (public, read-only)
whatever the caller sends
defaults as for r-universe



Everything below is read from bioc-registry at commit f10719e (main, 2026-09-28). A candidate propagates when every rule passes. Each decision returns every rule’s verdict, pass or fail, under these names:

build-status: the producer’s build status is success. For r-universe that is _status; _failure is not read. A green status on a stale commit is caught by version-gate in practice, because the stale version has already propagated. Before the gate runs, evaluate() drops any r-universe package with no source sha256.
families: at least one platform family passes, judged only on jobs running the gating R version. The gating R is resolved at evaluation time from bioconductor.org/config.yaml (r_ver_for_bioc_ver for the universe’s Bioconductor version) and matched against each job’s actual R version, not its label. Three families are gated (passingFamilies): linux (the source job plus linux-* x86_64), win (windows-* x86_64) and mac (macos-* arm64). A family passes when it has at least one gating job and none of them is ERROR, FAIL or FAILURE. NOTE and WARNING pass. Other configs gate nothing: bioc-checks, wasm, linux arm64, mac x86_64. bioc-build reports one linux-x86_64 job.
bioccheck: advisory in every caller today; it always passes and records the verdict. A caller could set it to blocking, and then ERROR/FAIL would block.
version-parse: the version is digits separated by . or -.
version-gate: the version is a strict bump over the one in the propagation index, or the package is new. A push without a bump never propagates. With replace_seed (bioc-build only), a build at the same version may also replace a bioconductor seed; r-universe must bump.
manifest-state, manifest-git-url, manifest-stream, manifest-component (bioc-build only): the package’s entry in bioc-manifest, read at the commit the build recorded, is active, names the git URL that was built, lists the build’s stream, and has component equal to profile.
deps, run last over everything the other rules cleared (approveByDeps): every Depends, Imports and LinkingTo entry naming a package that is itself in the propagation index must be present at a version meeting its >= or > constraint. Dependencies not in the index (CRAN, base R, and annotation, experiment and workflow packages until they have a build home) pass untouched. Candidates are approved in waves until a fixpoint, so a package lands as soon as what it waits on does. A dependency that is in neither the index nor CRAN is not caught; that is bioc-registry#56 (open), and finding 2 on Registry switch.

What propagates for an r-universe package that passes: the source tarball always; binaries only for the families that passed, and only those built at the same version with status success. wasm binaries ride along with no gate of their own. The passing families are recorded on the index entry as archs, the BiocCheck verdict as bioccheck.
Every new version that fails (its version-gate passed, something else did not) is written to prop/{universe}/blocked/ with its full list of rule verdicts. To ask why a package did not propagate, or whether it would, POST /gate runs the same function against the live index and writes nothing:
curl -s -X POST https://bioc-registry.seandavi.workers.dev/gate \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"universe":"bioc-release","candidates":[{"package":"limma","version":"99.0.0",
       "jobs":[{"config":"source","r":"4.6.0","check":"OK"}]}]}'
# 2026-09-30: propagate true, archs ["linux"], gating_r 4.6, "99.0.0 > 3.68.5"
What this gate does not check, and the legacy production gate or the push hooks do:

The nebbiolo1 sha match. The gate has no provenance check for r-universe builds. (bioc-build’s sha256 and gh attestation verify are checked by its publisher; per ADR 0011 they are integrity checks, not gate rules.)
The push-hook rules: version parity, x and y unchanged, the 5 MiB file limit, merge markers. It inherits them by trusting that the commit reached git.bioconductor.org.


Binaries that arrive after publication
The gate decides binaries in the wave that first publishes a version, and version-gate keeps that version out of every later wave. Since bioc-registry#50 (PR #51, merged 2026-09-29 02:30 UTC), every wave ends with a top-up (topUpBinaries, topUp):

For an r-universe entry, if r-universe now has a successful binary at the published version for a family that passed then or passes now on the gating R, it is added. This covers binaries that finish after the source was published and platforms whose check passes on a same-version rebuild.
For a seeded entry, Bioconductor’s binaries are fetched once they reach the seeded version.

Top-up is additive only: the source, its sha256 and the version never change, a family that passed is never withdrawn, and a slot that already has a binary keeps it. Each addition is recorded under prop/{universe}/topup/. POST /topup (maintenance key) runs the same for a backfill.

title: The propagation gate: what bioc-registry publishes, and why
text:
Three ways into the index
Each index entry carries an origin:









origin
How it got there
bioc (devel)
bioc-release




r-universe (or no field: entries from before the field existed)
passed the gate above; archs says on which families
2,292
2,235


bioconductor
seeded, never faced the gate; empty archs, null bioccheck
124
153


bioc-build
passed the gate through POST /publish
2
2



Counts from the live index, 2026-09-30.
Seeds exist because some packages build in BBS and fail in r-universe’s environment, usually because an example reaches a network service the runner cannot (about 300 when measured 2026-08-04; 277 seeded entries today). They are copied from Bioconductor’s repository for the universe’s branch: the devel repository for bioc, the release repository for bioc-release (seedPlan() in src/index.ts). Seeding only fills holes. A seed is replaced by an r-universe build when the maintainer bumps the version, or by a bioc-build build at the same version.

title: The propagation gate: what bioc-registry publishes, and why
text:
What r-universe already computes
A common assumption, encouraged by “r-universe doesn’t care about R CMD check”, is that r-universe skips checking. It does not. It does not gate on the result, which is a different claim. It runs R CMD check on every platform in its matrix, and for Bioconductor packages it also runs BiocCheck.
All of it is exposed in the per-package API, e.g. https://bioc.r-universe.dev/api/packages/limma (verified live, 2026-08-04):







Field
Contents




_jobs[]
one entry per matrix leg: {job, time, config, r, check, artifact}. config values include source, bioc-checks, linux-{devel,release}-{arm64,x86_64}, macos-*, windows-*, wasm-release. check is OK / NOTE / WARNING / ERROR / FAIL.


_bioccheck
BiocCheck summary as counts: {error, warning, note}. First-class API field; no download required.


_commit
{id, author, committer, message, time}: the source commit sha and metadata.


_status
overall deploy status for the package.


_failure
present when the newest commit failed to produce a source package.


_buildurl
the GitHub Actions run URL, in r-universe/{universe}.


_binaries[]
per-artifact provenance: {r, os, arch, distro, version, date, commit, fileid, status, check, buildurl}.



Build logs and the full BiocCheck artifact are retrievable without authentication via /api/actions/logs/{job} and /api/actions/artifacts/{id} (both 302 to a signed blob URL).
The gate therefore does not need to run checks. It needs to read them.

title: The propagation gate: what bioc-registry publishes, and why
text:
Why the registry polls
r-universe emits no webhook, no repository_dispatch, and no subscribable status endpoint. The feature request for build notifications (r-universe-org/help#101) is open with no comments (checked 2026-09-30). The one push-style signal, a GitHub commit status on the upstream repo (context r-universe/{universe}/{package}/deploy), needs the r-universe GitHub App installed on that repo; checked against bioc/limma on 2026-08-04 at the sha r-universe built, there were no statuses.
So the registry polls. Its Worker cron runs every 15 minutes (*/15 * * * * in wrangler.jsonc). Each run fetches /api/packages for both universes with a fixed field list and hashes the response; a new wave (gate, propagate, top-up) starts only when the hash changes. The field list leaves out volatile fields such as _stars so the hash stays quiet when nothing build-relevant changed. The same cron also captures logs and compacts the observation archive.
For scale: r-universe discovers new commits once an hour (sync.yml in r-universe-org/control-room, cron 25 * * * *, checked 2026-09-30), and rebuilds nightly (rebuilds.yml, 30 1 * * *). Measured against bioc-release on 2026-08-04, /api/files with fields=_created,_buildurl,_commit was 1.1 MB in 0.27 s; /api/packages with a field list 6.4 MB in 0.9 s; with no field list about 69 MB. Always pass fields=. PATCH /api/sync is public, unauthenticated, and self-throttles to 60 seconds, if a sync is needed ahead of the cron.

Two traps in the data
_status can be green on a stale commit. When the newest commit fails to produce a source package, the package keeps its previous successful _status and the failure appears separately in _failure. A gate reading only _status will propagate while the current head is broken. This gate reads only _status and relies on version-gate (rule 1 above).
Key the delta on _commit.id, not build time. 453 release packages were rebuilt in the 24 hours before the 2026-08-04 measurement, but r-universe also rebuilds on dependency changes, R-version changes, the nightly rebuild cron, and a reverse-dependency cascade after any version change. Most of that churn carries no new source.

title: Size limits in the r-universe build
text:
NoteA dated reading of code, not a published specification



r-universe does not document a size limit anywhere on docs.r-universe.dev. Everything on this page was read on 2026-09-02 from the workflow that actually runs: r-universe-org/workflows at ref v3, r-universe-org/actions at ref v12, and r-universe-org/build-source at 1ee4788. The measurements of BiocCheck’s behaviour were made against BiocCheck 1.49.30. Any of this can change without notice; the point of citing line numbers is that it can be re-checked rather than believed.
Bioconductor’s builds are moving to r-universe, which makes r-universe’s constraints Bioconductor’s constraints. The most consequential one is a limit on how large a package may be — the constraint that stalled the proposal to add data and workflow packages to the Bioconductor universes.
Three different systems impose size limits on a Bioconductor package, and two of them use the number 100, which makes them easy to conflate. They apply to different objects at different moments, and a package can satisfy any one of them while failing another. This page states what each one is.

title: Size limits in the r-universe build
text:
Three limits, three different objects



Limit
Applies to
Enforced by
At what moment




104,857,600 bytes
one built package file (source .tar.gz or one platform binary)
r-universe build workflow
after the package is built, before upload


104,857,600 bytes
one file inside a git push
GitHub’s git server
on git push


5,242,880 bytes
one file inside a git push, software packages only
Bioconductor’s pre-receive hook
on git push to git.bioconductor.org


10,000,000 bytes
source tarball, software packages only
BiocCheck (ERROR)
during check — but see below


5,000,000 bytes
one file inside the package
BiocCheck (WARNING)
during check — but see below



The distinction that matters most: the first row is measured on a compressed archive that the build produced, and the second and third are measured on individual files as stored in git. A repository of forty 20 MB files passes every git-side check and fails r-universe. A single 500 MB file tracked in Git LFS passes r-universe’s git-side concerns entirely and can never be built into a package small enough to publish.

title: Size limits in the r-universe build
text:
Where r-universe’s limit lives
The same check appears twice, written the same way both times:



Stage
Location
Scope




End of the source build
build-source/entrypoint.sh:347
the finished source .tar.gz


Every artifact upload
actions/store-package/action.yml:38
source and every binary — linux, Windows, macOS, wasm



The second is reached from six places in the build workflow (build.yml at ref v3, lines 95, 105, 165, 229, 292 and 339), which is every target r-universe publishes. The only artifact that bypasses it is the BiocCheck output directory, uploaded directly at line 383.
Both are one line of shell:
if [ -n "$(find "$FILE" -prune -size +100M)" ]; then
  echo "File $FILE is larger than 100 MB. This is not allowed"
  exit 1
fi

The number is 100 MiB, not 100 MB
The message says “100 MB”, but find -size +100M counts in 1 MiB units and rounds each file up to the next whole unit before comparing. The effective rule is therefore:

A file fails if it is strictly larger than 104,857,600 bytes.

Checked against GNU findutils 4.8.0: 104,857,600 bytes passes, 104,857,601 bytes is rejected, and a file of 100,000,000 bytes — 100 MB in the decimal sense — passes with 4.8 MiB to spare. The gap between the two readings is about 4.9%, which is enough to matter for a package sitting near the line.


What is being measured
The source-package check runs after r-universe has appended its own files to the tarball — the rendered README, the HTML manual, citation files and contents.json are unpacked into the archive at entrypoint.sh:341-343, immediately before the size check at line 347. A package’s budget is therefore not what R CMD build produced locally; it is that, plus r-universe’s additions, recompressed.





flowchart TB
  C["git clone"] --> B["R CMD build<br/>vignettes, no manual"]
  B --> X["append r-universe extras<br/>README · HTML manual · citation · contents.json"]
  X --> G1{"> 104,857,600 bytes?"}
  G1 -->|"yes"| F1["exit 1 — source job fails<br/>nothing is published"]
  G1 -->|"no"| S["source package"]
  S --> BIN["binary builds<br/>linux · win · mac · wasm"]
  BIN --> G2{"> 104,857,600 bytes?"}
  G2 -->|"yes"| F2["exit 1 — that platform fails<br/>source still deploys"]
  G2 -->|"no"| U["uploaded and published"]

  classDef ok fill:#f3fbf4,stroke:#3d8b47,color:#12263f
  classDef gate fill:#fff8e6,stroke:#b8860b,color:#12263f
  classDef bad fill:#fff1f0,stroke:#c0392b,color:#12263f
  class C,B,X,S,BIN,U ok
  class G1,G2 gate
  class F1,F2 bad






The two failures are not equivalent. An oversized source package fails before entrypoint.sh writes its SOURCEPKG output, and every downstream job in the workflow is conditioned on that output being non-empty — so the package is not built for any platform, not checked, and not published at all. An oversized binary fails only its own job; the source package and the other platforms still deploy.


What r-universe does not limit
No limit was found on any of: the size of individual files inside a package, the total size of a universe, the number of packages in a universe, vignette or documentation output, or the BiocCheck results artifact. Within the 100 MiB per-file ceiling, a universe is unbounded as far as the build code is concerned.
One related constant is worth knowing about, because it is a size decision even though it is not a size check. build-source/R/buildtools.R:395 carries a hard-coded list of four packages commented “Packages over 2GB in size” — SNPlocs.Hsapiens.dbSNP155.GRCh38, SNPlocs.Hsapiens.dbSNP155.GRCh37, MafDb.gnomAD.r2.1.GRCh38 and MafDb.gnomAD.r2.1.hs37d5 — which are never installed as dependencies. A package that depends on one of them is built without it, and whatever that does to its checks is what its check results report.

title: Size limits in the r-universe build
text:
What GitHub imposes
These are GitHub’s platform limits, not r-universe’s choices. They constrain the build because the build runs on GitHub Actions and clones from GitHub.







Constraint
Value




File in a push — hard block
100 MiB


File in a push — warning
50 MiB


File uploaded via the web UI
25 MiB


Git LFS, per file
2 GB (Free/Pro), 4 GB (Team), 5 GB (Enterprise Cloud)


Repository size
under 1 GB ideal, under 5 GB strongly recommended (advisory)


Actions artifact, per artifact
no documented limit — only a shared storage quota, 500 MB (Free) to 50 GB (Enterprise Cloud)


Artifacts per job
500


Artifact retention
90 days by default


Job execution time
6 hours


Standard runner
4 cores, 16 GB RAM, 14 GB SSD



r-universe sets its own timeouts well inside GitHub’s: 60 minutes for a source build (90 for Bioconductor), 150-minute caps on the platform jobs, and a 50-minute timeout around R CMD build itself. The workflow also deletes the preinstalled .NET, GHC and Boost trees before building, which is what a 14 GB disk looks like in practice.

title: Size limits in the r-universe build
text:
Where the limits genuinely differ
The two 100 MiB numbers are unrelated. They coincide numerically and share no scope. GitHub’s applies to a single blob entering git history; r-universe’s applies to a compressed archive leaving the build. Neither implies the other in either direction.
GitHub does not limit artifact size at all. r-universe’s ceiling is entirely self-imposed — GitHub would accept the upload. The limit is a statement about what r-universe is willing to store and serve, so it is a policy that can be discussed, not a platform constraint that has to be worked around.
r-universe has no per-file rule; Bioconductor’s rules are all per-file. Bioconductor’s pre-receive hook and BiocCheck both police individual files and are indifferent to the total; r-universe polices only the total and is indifferent to how it is distributed.
Git size and tarball size are not the same quantity. r-universe clones the full history (the clone at entrypoint.sh:43 is deliberately not shallow, so that vignette modification times can be read), so a small package with a heavy history costs the build real time and disk while passing the size gate untouched. The size audit found depmap shipping a 1.6 MiB tarball behind a 1.51 GiB git repository.
The limit is undocumented. For a maintainer, the only signal is a failed build log reading File <pkg>.tar.gz is larger than 100 MB. This is not allowed.

title: Size limits in the r-universe build
section: Bioconductor’s own size rules are silent in this pipeline
text:
Bioconductor’s own size rules are silent in this pipeline
Bioconductor’s stated guidance is a 10 MB source tarball for software packages (experiment and annotation packages are exempt) and 5 MB per individual file, enforced through BiocCheck. The r-universe workflow runs BiocCheck for the Bioconductor universes, so it is reasonable to assume those rules are being applied there. They are not.
BiocCheck is invoked on the built tarball. Three things follow from that, all confirmed by running BiocCheck 1.49.30 on a purpose-built 30 MB package containing a single 30 MB file in inst/extdata:

checkPackageSize() measures file.size() of the package’s sourceDir field. For tarball input that field holds the directory the tarball was unpacked into, so file.size() returns a directory entry size — 83 bytes in the test — and the 10 MB comparison can never be true. The same is true for source-directory input, where the field holds the source directory itself.
checkIndivFileSizes() and checkDataFileSizes() both delegate to a helper with two branches, one for a git clone and one for a source directory. Tarball input is neither, so the helper returns nothing. On source-directory input it works correctly and did find the 30 MB file.
A full BiocCheck() run on the 30 MB tarball reported 2 errors and 2 warnings, none of them about size.

So in the r-universe Bioconductor jobs, the only size limit in force is r-universe’s own 104,857,600 bytes — roughly ten times Bioconductor’s stated tarball guidance, and with no per-file component at all. This has been reported upstream as Bioconductor/BiocCheck#259.
The Bioconductor rule that is enforced today is the 5,242,880-byte pre-receive hook on git.bioconductor.org, described in the propagation gate. That hook runs on push, before r-universe is involved at all, and it covers software packages only. Nothing in the r-universe path reproduces it — which matters for any plan that treats r-universe’s checks as a replacement for the git server’s.

title: Size limits in the r-universe build
section: What this means for the migration
text:
What this means for the migration
The size audit put numbers to the consequences: 67 of 434 experiment-data packages and 1 of 25 workflow packages exceed the limit, against exactly one software package (SwathXtend) in the current release. The limit is therefore invisible to the software corpus and decisive for the data corpus, which is why it surfaced only when adding data packages was proposed.
Two properties of the limit are worth carrying into that discussion. It is a policy of r-universe’s, not a GitHub constraint, so it is negotiable in a way platform limits are not. And it measures the wrong thing for the packages it excludes: the cost r-universe actually bears for a large data package is dominated by cloning a large git repository and by storing 8–14 near-identical binaries, neither of which the tarball size predicts.






WarningOne thing that was not verified



Neither r-universe-org/base-image nor build-source installs git-lfs, and the clone at entrypoint.sh:43 is a plain git clone --recurse-submodules. On that reading, a repository whose data files are tracked in Git LFS would be checked out as pointer files and built into a package that is small, valid, and missing its data — while buildtools.R:962 records gitlfs: true in the package metadata without failing anything. This was not tested against a live build, and it should be before anyone relies on it either way.

title: Size limits in the r-universe build
text:
Reproducing this
The r-universe boundary, against GNU findutils 4.8.0:
head -c 104857600 /dev/zero > f1   # exactly 100 MiB
head -c 104857601 /dev/zero > f2   # one byte more
find f1 -prune -size +100M         # no output — passes
find f2 -prune -size +100M         # prints f2 — rejected
The BiocCheck behaviour, given any source package directory with a file over 5 MB in inst/extdata:
R CMD build bigpkg    # produces bigpkg_0.99.0.tar.gz, ~30 MB

bp <- BiocCheck:::.BiocPackage$copy()
bp$initialize("bigpkg_0.99.0.tar.gz")
bp$isTar                                          # TRUE
file.size(bp$sourceDir)                           # 83 — a directory, not the tarball
file.size(bp$tarFilename)                         # 30005481 — the tarball
BiocCheck:::checkPackageSize(bp)                  # silent
BiocCheck:::.findLargeFiles(bp, data_only = FALSE) # NULL

bp2 <- BiocCheck:::.BiocPackage$copy()
bp2$initialize("bigpkg")                          # the source directory
BiocCheck:::.findLargeFiles(bp2, data_only = FALSE) # finds inst/extdata/blob.bin
BiocCheck:::checkPackageSize(bp2)                  # still silent

title: Serving software packages from the registry
text:
NoteStatus: proposed; step 0 in progress (updated 2026-09-30)



Step 0 has two of its four items done: binaries are re-evaluated on every wave and seed binaries refresh (bioc-registry#51, merged 2026-09-29). The dependency gate rule and keeping bioc-build output out of the software index are open. Steps 1–5 have not started, and none of the decisions below is made.
A plan for making bioconductor.org’s software repositories come from bioc-registry, which is built from r-universe, instead of from the legacy build system (BBS). Every step and every test below cites the measurement that makes it necessary. Measurements are from 2026-09-28 unless another date is given, and are reproducible with the scripts in evidence/registry-switch/. Tracked in bioc-infrastructure#35.

title: Serving software packages from the registry
section: Where software packages come from today
text:
Where software packages come from today
bioconductor.org is served by the new edge, but its package repositories are still an hourly mirror of the legacy docroot. The Worker serves /packages/... from R2, which the edge’s sync job fills from that docroot. It never reads from the registry.








On bioconductor.org
Sample
Built by




Release (3.23) source tarballs
20 of 20
BBS (packaged by biocbuild)


Devel (3.24) source tarballs
10 of 10
BBS (biocbuild)


Release Windows binaries
15 of 15
r-universe (carry r-universe’s RemoteSha)


Release macOS binary (limma)
1
r-universe



So Windows and macOS users already install r-universe builds, reaching bioconductor.org through the core team’s propagation, which only publishes an r-universe build whose version and commit match what the BBS host nebbiolo1 built (legacy propagation). Anyone installing from source (Linux, most CI, containers) gets BBS tarballs.
Separately, the registry already runs a complete r-universe-built repository, gated by its own propagation gate, at https://bioc-registry.seandavi.workers.dev/repo/{bioc-release,bioc}. Nothing on bioconductor.org uses it yet. Switching bioconductor.org to it is the step that takes BBS out of the path for software packages.

title: Serving software packages from the registry
text:
What the switch covers








Path under /packages/<ver>/bioc/
After the switch
Why




src/contrib/ tarballs and PACKAGES, .gz, .rds
registry
the install path

registry

VIEWS

Only the current release (3.23) and devel (3.24). Older releases are archival (ADR 0006) and stay as they are; they are 77% of package traffic, so most installs are unaffected either way. Annotation, experiment and workflow repositories stay on the mirror until bioc-build covers them.

title: Serving software packages from the registry
section: Findings: what would regress if we switched today
text:
Findings: what would regress if we switched today
Compared file by file, the registry and bioconductor.org agree on almost everything: for release, 2,374 of 2,384 source packages at the same version. The differences below are the ones that matter. Request counts are from about 70 minutes of post-cutover access logs, with a blocked crawler excluded.
1. No PACKAGES.rds. The registry serves PACKAGES and PACKAGES.gz but answers 404 for PACKAGES.rds, for source and every binary directory. It’s the index R asks for first, and the most requested: 2,784 requests against about 220 for .gz and plain PACKAGES. R falls back to the next format, so installs keep working, but every repository lookup pays an extra round trip. Blocking.
2. Packages that can’t be installed. The registry serves 6 release and 13 devel packages that bioconductor.org doesn’t, such as Ularcirc, SNPhood, progeny and sparrow. They are still in Bioconductor’s manifest and in r-universe, but a hard dependency was removed from Bioconductor (decoupleR, BiocSet, Organism.dplyr, BPRMeth), so BBS stopped propagating them. Checked with tools::package_dependencies over the repository plus CRAN and the data repositories, the registry adds 4 release and 7 devel packages whose hard dependencies can’t be resolved, on top of bioconductor.org’s own (9 release, 2 devel, all CRAN packages that were archived). A user asking for one gets a confusing failure instead of “not available”. Blocking. The fix is a gate rule, not a list: don’t publish a package whose hard dependencies aren’t resolvable.
3. Versions that fail in r-universe lag. 153 release and 124 devel entries were seeded once from Bioconductor’s own builds for packages that fail in r-universe’s environment. A seed is replaced only when r-universe builds a newer version that passes the gate. Today 3 release and 8 devel packages are behind bioconductor.org, including biomaRt, DOSE and CNVRanger. Asked through the registry’s own POST /gate, every one of them is blocked by a rule, which is what the gate is for: the newer version fails to build in r-universe (biomaRt 2.69.4, bedbaser, CNVRanger, knowYourCG, alabaster.vcf; SwathXtend, whose 346 MB tarball has no successful build), or it builds but its checks ERROR on every platform (DOSE 4.7.3, MsBackendMetaboLights 1.7.8). PIPETS is the same case one step removed: r-universe’s last successful build is 1.7.0, and its 1.9.0 build failed. BBS publishes these versions because they pass in BBS’s environment. The gate is stricter than BBS here, and after a switch those packages’ bug-fix releases would wait until they pass in r-universe. A decision, not a fix: accept the lag (and chase the failures with the maintainers), or bridge by re-seeding from BBS, which keeps BBS in the path for those packages.
4. Missing binaries. These counts compare the registry’s repository with bioconductor.org; bioconductor.org itself is not missing these binaries. On 2026-09-28, before the fix described below, for release the registry lacked 61 Windows, 49 macOS arm64 and 76 macOS Intel binaries that bioconductor.org serves (devel: 48, 57, 72), 363 in all. The gate publishes a binary only for a platform whose r-universe check has no ERROR or FAIL on the gating R line, and seeds copy a binary only if bioconductor.org’s binary matches the source version. Classifying every one of the 363 against those rules (binwhy.py, 2026-09-28):








Cause
Count
Verdict




The platform’s check fails in r-universe (e.g. KEGGREST on Windows, BiocParallel on macOS)
114
by design


Not in the source repository at all; bioconductor.org serves a binary for a package it no longer lists as source (e.g. BiRewire)
26
by design


Seed, and bioconductor.org’s binary is older than its own source (e.g. Windows AnnotationForge 1.53.0 next to source 1.54.0)
58
by design


Seed, and bioconductor.org’s binary has since caught up to the seeded version (seeds never refresh)
12
gap


Seed whose version lags bioconductor.org
2
follows finding 3


Withheld when first published; r-universe has rebuilt the same version since, and it now passes (e.g. ChIPpeakAnno on macOS, OGRE on Windows)
107
bug


The platform passed, but the binary wasn’t built yet when the source was published, and is never added later (e.g. SparseArray: published Sept 23, binaries built Sept 24)
30
bug


Withheld; r-universe has since moved to a newer version that isn’t published
14
follows finding 3



The two bugs have one cause: the gate decides a package’s binaries once, when its version is first published, and never looks again at that version. So 137 binaries that the registry’s own rules would admit today are missing (bioc-registry#50). Fixed and backfilled in bioc-registry#51: re-running the comparison, the missing binaries fell from 363 to 222, the bug rows from 137 to 8, and the seed-refresh row by 12. None of the 8 left has an r-universe binary to add (a macOS Intel build failed or doesn’t exist, or the binary hasn’t been built yet for a version published an hour earlier). Was blocking: re-evaluate the binaries of each published version on every r-universe wave, adding any whose platform now passes (the source and the version stay as they are).
The “by design” rows change what users get: in 88 of the 363 (2026-09-28; not re-counted after the fix), bioconductor.org serves a binary older than its source (BBS keeps the last binary that built). After a switch, a Windows or macOS user gets a source install of the current version instead of an older binary, which fails for a package with compiled code on a machine without a toolchain. That is a policy choice to make explicitly (see decisions).
5. No Archive/. The registry keeps only the current version. src/contrib/Archive/ on bioconductor.org served 886 requests (renv restores and remotes::install_version) in the sample. At first it stays on the mirror; once BBS stops producing it, superseded registry tarballs have to be archived by whatever writes the repository. Blocking for detaching BBS, not for the switch.
6. Data and workflow packages in the software repository. The registry has two universes, bioc and bioc-release, and bioc-build publishes into them, so msdata (experiment data), rnaseqDTU (a workflow) and ARRmData appear in the software PACKAGES. Blocking. They belong in data/experiment and workflows.
7. Missing index fields. PACKAGES lacks MD5sum, Archs, License_is_FOSS and License_restricts_use; VIEWS lacks those plus dependencyCount, Rfiles, hasNEWS, organism, PackageStatus and others. No consumer of MD5sum is confirmed. Writing the indexes with R’s tools::write_PACKAGES() from the actual tarballs produces the PACKAGES fields for free. Not blocking; the VIEWS fields are checked against the site build.
8. Same version, different build. For 33 release packages both sides have the same version but different contents: bioconductor.org declares R (>= 4.6), the registry R (>= 4.5). The maintainer changed DESCRIPTION without a version bump, and the registry kept the first build of that version, as its gate intends. Installing on R 4.6 is unaffected. Expected; the tests must allow it.
9. The registry is not built to serve at edge speed. Its indexes are generated per request with cache-control: no-store and take 250–550 ms; bioconductor.org serves the same files from the edge cache in about 60–85 ms (2026-09-28). Re-measured 2026-09-30 from onclappc02 with a new connection per request: 210–240 ms for a cached PACKAGES from bioconductor.org, 440–480 ms from the registry. The index changes a few times a day for release and about ten times a day for devel. This decides the mechanism below.

title: Serving software packages from the registry
section: Mechanism: write the registry’s repository into the edge’s storage
text:
Mechanism: write the registry’s repository into the edge’s storage
Two ways to serve it:

Proxy: the Worker forwards /packages/3.2x/bioc/src/… to the registry at request time. Every index request would take the registry’s latency or need a new caching and purge scheme, and bioconductor.org installs would depend on the registry Worker being up.
Materialize (recommended): a job writes the registry’s repository into the same R2 keys the mirror writes today (packages/3.24/bioc/src/contrib/…), generating PACKAGES, .gz and .rds with tools::write_PACKAGES() from the tarballs, and purges the changed keys with the existing cf_purge_keys. The Worker, its cache rules, 404 caching, logs, and the mirror manifest need no change. The hourly sync stops writing those paths (an rsync-filter exclusion), and turning that exclusion off again is the rollback.

This follows the rule the estate already has: producers publish into storage, and the edge decides what to serve (contract 3 on the overview).

title: Serving software packages from the registry
text:
Plan
Each step names its rollback. Nothing moves to the next step until its tests pass.
0. Fix the blocking gaps in the registry.

Gate rule: a package is published only if its hard dependencies resolve within the repository, CRAN and the Bioconductor data repositories (finding 2).
Binaries: re-evaluate the binaries of each published version on every wave, so a platform that passes later, or a binary built after the source was published, is added (finding 4: 137 binaries; bioc-registry#50). Done.
Repository type: route bioc-build output into data and workflow repositories, never the software index (finding 6).
Seeds: refresh a seed’s binaries when bioconductor.org’s catch up to the seeded version (finding 4: 12 binaries; also bioc-registry#50). Done. Whether to re-seed newer versions from BBS is a decision (finding 3).

1. Build the materializer, writing to a staging prefix. It writes the full software tree for 3.23 and 3.24 under a prefix the Worker doesn’t serve (for example staging/registry/), on every registry index change. Rollback: nothing is served from it.
2. Serve the staging tree on the rehearsal host. next.bioconductor.org gets a route that maps /packages/3.2x/bioc/{src,bin,VIEWS} to the staging prefix, the same mechanism as the strangler route table. Run every test below against next. for at least a week of registry updates. Rollback: remove the route.
3. Flip devel (3.24) on bioconductor.org. Devel is 2% of package traffic and its users expect movement. The materializer writes the production keys for 3.24; the hourly sync excludes them. Watch the logs for 404s and for installs of packages that used to exist. Hold for a week. Rollback: remove the exclusion, run the sync, purge.
4. Flip release (3.23). Same steps, after devel has been clean for a week. Rollback: same.
5. Archive. Before BBS stops producing Archive/, the materializer moves superseded tarballs into Archive/<pkg>/ (finding 5).
After step 4, BBS is out of the install path for software packages, except for any seeds that are still bridged (finding 3). The legacy docroot still supplies documentation files and older releases until M2 retires it.

title: Serving software packages from the registry
text:
Decisions needed
Neither this page nor #35 names who makes these decisions or by when (checked 2026-09-30).

Lagging versions (finding 3): accept that versions failing in r-universe wait, or bridge them from BBS for now?
Stale binaries (finding 4): for a package whose current version fails on a platform, bioconductor.org serves an older binary today. After the switch, users on that platform get a source install of the current version. Accept, or also publish the last binary that passed?
Mirror operators keep syncing from the legacy host, so after the flip they would serve BBS builds while bioconductor.org serves registry builds. Point them at the manifest-based mirror guide first, or accept the divergence for a while?
Documentation files (vignettes/ and the rest) stay on BBS’s output, so for a package where the two builds differ, its vignette can come from a different build than its tarball. Acceptable until the site build produces them?

title: Reproducing the package pages
text:
NotePart of the migration record

The package landing pages are the largest part of bioconductor.org — roughly 92,000 of them across every release still published. This page records what it takes to reproduce them without the legacy build hosts, what has actually been demonstrated, and what has not.
Measurements are from 2026-08-03. Companion pages: VIEWS & r-universe for the data-source analysis, Builder Transition for the wider build-system picture.

The short version
Every package page for releases 2.5 through 3.24 can be regenerated today with no access to master, staging, or any build machine. The inputs are two published JSON artifacts plus a public git clone.

Three things this table is meant to stop anyone assuming:
r-universe does not cover Bioconductor. It covers software packages. There is no universe for annotation, experiment or workflows — every candidate hostname 404s — so a third of the corpus has no origin outside the site. The remaining source for those is the DESCRIPTION file inside ~1,392 package tarballs.
Rank has an independent origin but no independent path. bio-web-stats runs on a VPC-private host, reachable only because master reverse-proxies /packages/stats/ to it. Retiring master takes the stats offline while the application carries on running. Its own upstream is CloudFront logs in an S3 bucket — and moving traffic to Cloudflare stops those logs being produced at all. See Download Stats for how that pipeline works and where it is currently producing wrong numbers.
Repository artifacts have an origin, just not one we have wired up. MD5sum and the binary paths come from the package repository’s own PACKAGES index and directory listing, not from any build machine. MD5sum in particular is read by nothing and can be dropped.

title: Reproducing the package pages
text:
tree.json: the category hierarchy
tree.json drives the package category browser, and it regenerates exactly — 500 of 500 nodes identical to the published file for both 3.23 and 3.24, labels and package lists alike; 496 of 496 for 3.18. It needs two inputs, neither of which touches a build machine: the term hierarchy from Bioconductor/biocViews (inst/dot/biocViewsVocab.dot, the editable DOT source) and the biocViews field on each package.
Its sibling biocViews.json — the same taxonomy as a flat map of 501 nodes — is read by nothing. Its own source in get_json.rb is marked todo - remove this, and it does not need generating.
Three details are worth recording, because each of them silently produced wrong output first.
A node’s two package figures are different sets. packageList holds packages filed directly under a term; the count shown in data is cumulative over the whole subtree. So AssayDomain renders as "AssayDomain (960)" while carrying only 13 packages. Treating both as cumulative put 26 nodes out.
Some terms have no direct assignments at all. ChipManufacturer and ChipName are never declared by any package — annotation packages name the child term (CodelinkChip, adme16cod) and skip the parent — yet the published output fills them cumulatively. Terms with no direct assignments but populated descendants therefore fall back to the cumulative set.
The vocabulary must be pinned per release. Terms are added over time, so devel’s list applied to an older release invents categories that did not exist then. Using devel against 3.18 produced four spurious terms; pinning to RELEASE_3_18 made it exact. This shows up as a gradient rather than an error — 3.10 matched 473 of 475 nodes, 2.9 only 202 of 243 — which is exactly the kind of drift that looks like success if you only check the current release. biocViews release branches reach back only to RELEASE_3_7; older releases fall back to devel with a warning and carry extra terms.
The node format itself is not uniform:
{"data": "GeneExpression (639)",
 "attr": {"packageList": "a4Classif,acde,ADAM,…", "id": "GeneExpression"},
 "children": []}

{"data": "MetagenomeAssembly", "childnum": 0, "children": []}
Terms with packages carry attr and a count in data; empty terms carry childnum: 0 and a bare name.

title: Reproducing the package pages
section: Much of the data is never read
text:
Much of the data is never read
An audit of every consumer — the Nanoc data source, Rules, the five package-page layout components, and the helpers they call — found a large part of the record has no consumer at all: MD5sum, NeedsCompilation, git_url, git_last_commit, git_last_commit_date, Date/Publication, VignetteBuilder, OS_type, License_is_FOSS, License_restricts_use and organism. A generator does not need to produce any of them.
Constraints a generator must honour:

The top level is a JSON object keyed by package name. That key alone determines the page URL; get it wrong and every URL changes.
Twelve fields are arrays, the four has* fields are JSON booleans, Rank is an integer and dependencyCount is a string of digits.
The category browser reads a Rake-derived packages.js whose rows are positional — [Package, Maintainer, Title, Rank, dependencyCount], indices 0–3 read by position. Reordering silently breaks search and autocomplete.
URL is dereferenced without a nil guard, so omit the key rather than emitting null.

title: Reproducing the package pages
text:
Status
Demonstrated:

Package pages for 35 releases build from published JSON with no Bioconductor host access.
Two independent renderers produce identical URLs from the same contract.
Software-package metadata regenerates from r-universe.
Reverse dependencies regenerate from the four repositories plus CRAN — folding CRAN in matters, without it limma alone was missing 42 importsMe entries.
tree.json regenerates exactly for current releases, from the biocViews vocabulary and the package metadata.

Not demonstrated:

Regenerating packages.json for annotation, experiment or workflow packages from anything but the site. This is the largest remaining gap: 1,392 packages, roughly a third of the current corpus.
Any independent path to Rank.
Regenerating historical releases’ JSON — r-universe holds only current release and devel, so for 2.5–3.22 the published JSON may simply be the archival record, in which case snapshotting it is the right answer rather than regeneration.
